bullets: MultiAgentInject is a new security benchmark with 4,050 trials that independently varies task, agent-network topology, attack class, stealth, and propagation depth. It records whether an injected instruction reaches other agents separately from whether those agents comply, rather than collapsing both events into attack success. Why it matters: If you are evaluating multi-agent defenses, this separation helps identify whether to change communication boundaries that permit propagation or safeguards that prevent compliance after exposure. A single attack-success score cannot distinguish those decisions. Evidence: E002. High confidence.

SimGlot is a new artifact for testing the benchmark harness itself—the task generator and reward function that decide whether an agent succeeded. It provides eight integrity checks and 21 injected fault variants across seven defect classes, with records binding results to frozen software revisions. Why it matters: If you maintain an agent benchmark, this offers a way to test whether scores survive known evaluator defects before using them for model selection. It shifts part of evaluation from testing agents to verifying that the scoring software supplies a trustworthy answer key. Evidence: E056. High confidence.

APEX-Harm is a new prompt- and script-injection benchmark for long-running agents operating across shared professional workspaces. Its finance, consulting, and legal tasks contain 115 to 328 files and expose email, calendar, chat, documents, spreadsheets, Portable Document Format files, and code execution through tool servers. Why it matters: If you are testing workplace agents, this means defenses can be assessed when malicious material may appear anywhere in a large, changing workspace—not only at a predetermined document location. That design better distinguishes safe navigation across tools from resistance to one isolated prompt. Evidence: E024. High confidence.

MisVisAgentBench is a new executable web-agent benchmark containing 280 matched pairs of clean and misleading charts. The pairing holds the task context together while changing the visualization, then measures effects on downstream agent actions rather than chart-question accuracy alone. Why it matters: If you are choosing a web-agent evaluation, matched pairs let you attribute execution changes to misleading visual evidence more directly than unrelated task sets can. The benchmark also tests whether chart interpretation errors propagate into actions, which matters for agents that act on dashboards. Evidence: E029. High confidence.

CRBugBench is a new code-review benchmark built from 1,000 human-verified bugs across 98 open-source repositories. Each task pairs a bug with the pull request that introduced it, turning repository history into a review task rather than asking an agent to generate code from scratch. Why it matters: If you are deciding whether automated review can supervise agent-written code, this evaluates detection of defects that passed through real development workflows. It measures a different deployment gate from coding benchmarks: whether a reviewer catches an introduced bug before approval. Evidence: E022. High confidence.

CACE-Bench is a new synthetic benchmark and generator for credit-processing agents under auditability constraints. Its regulatory-shift track separates the applicants used to admit pipeline changes from the 300 applicants evaluated per seed, and it reports admissions of candidate changes and harmful changes separately. Why it matters: If you are evaluating an agent that modifies a regulated decision pipeline, the held-out gate tests whether proposed changes generalize beyond the cases used to approve them. Separate harmful-admission reporting also supports a release decision that ordinary average performance would obscure. Evidence: E004. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: MultiAgentInject 是一个新的安全基准，包含 4,050 次试验，可独立改变任务、智能体网络拓扑、攻击类别、隐蔽性和传播深度。它分别记录注入指令是否到达其他智能体，以及这些智能体是否遵从指令，而不是将这两个事件合并为攻击成功。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估多智能体防御，这种区分有助于判断应调整允许传播的通信边界，还是应改进防止智能体在接触攻击后遵从指令的防护措施。单一的攻击成功分数无法区分这些决策。Evidence: E002. High confidence.

SimGlot 是一个用于测试基准测试工具本身的新制品——即用于判定智能体是否成功的任务生成器和奖励函数。它提供八项完整性检查，并覆盖七类缺陷的 21 种注入故障变体，同时通过记录将结果与冻结的软件修订版本绑定。Why it matters: 如果你负责维护智能体基准，它提供了一种方法，可在使用分数进行模型选择之前，测试这些分数能否经受住已知评估器缺陷的影响。它将评估的一部分重点从测试智能体转向验证评分软件能否提供可信的标准答案。Evidence: E056. High confidence.

APEX-Harm 是一个新的提示注入和脚本注入基准，面向在共享专业工作空间中长期运行的智能体。其金融、咨询和法律任务包含 115 至 328 个文件，并通过工具服务器开放电子邮件、日历、聊天、文档、电子表格、Portable Document Format 文件和代码执行功能。Why it matters: 如果你正在测试工作场所智能体，这意味着可以在恶意材料可能出现在庞大且不断变化的工作空间中任何位置的情况下评估防御能力，而不只是在预先确定的文档位置进行评估。与抵御单个孤立提示相比，这种设计能更好地区分智能体能否安全地跨工具导航。Evidence: E024. High confidence.

MisVisAgentBench 是一个新的可执行网页智能体基准，包含 280 对相互匹配的正常图表和误导性图表。配对设计在改变可视化内容的同时保持任务情境一致，随后衡量其对智能体下游行动的影响，而不只衡量图表问答准确率。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择网页智能体评估，匹配对能比互不相关的任务集更直接地将执行变化归因于误导性视觉证据。该基准还测试图表解读错误是否会传导至行动，这对于依据仪表板采取行动的智能体至关重要。Evidence: E029. High confidence.

CRBugBench 是一个新的代码审查基准，由来自 98 个开源代码库、经人工验证的 1,000 个缺陷构建而成。每项任务都将一个缺陷与引入该缺陷的拉取请求配对，从而把代码库历史转化为审查任务，而不是要求智能体从头生成代码。Why it matters: 如果你正在判断自动化审查能否监督智能体编写的代码，该基准可以评估对那些曾通过真实开发工作流的缺陷的检测能力。它衡量的是一种不同于编码基准的部署关卡：审查者能否在批准前发现新引入的缺陷。Evidence: E022. High confidence.

CACE-Bench 是一个新的合成基准及生成器，面向受到可审计性约束的信贷处理智能体。其监管变化赛道将用于准入流程变更的申请人与每个种子下接受评估的 300 名申请人分开，并分别报告候选变更和有害变更的准入情况。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估会修改受监管决策流程的智能体，这一留出关卡可以测试所提变更能否泛化到批准这些变更时所用案例之外。单独报告有害变更的准入情况，也有助于做出普通平均性能会掩盖的发布决策。Evidence: E004. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Compliance-Aware Credit-agent Evaluation (CACE-Bench): a synthetic, reproducible benchmark and generator for evaluating LLM-agent credit pipelines, and the self-evolution of such pipelines, under auditability constraints. No production credit data is used; the only real records are the 1,000 applications of the public, anonymised Statlog German Credit data (UCI, CC BY 4.0), shipped with a SHA-256 check. Version 0.7.0 runs the regulatory-shift track on those applicants (evolve real.py; evolve.py unchanged) with a 700/300 split of applicants per seed, so no evaluated applicant is in the gate's pool. Over 90 runs the gated dual loop admitted 171 of 6874 candidate changes with 0 harmful admissions; the same loops without the gate admitted 228 harmful changes and ended with a missed-flag rate above 10 percent in 29 of 90 runs. The dual loop reached the oracle harness in 80 of 80 runs outside the scope-high cell and in 0 of 10 within it, where the fixed tolerance blocks the correct change (9 of 10 at epsilon = 0.01); there the residual false positives fall unevenly, by +2.3 percentage points for women and +4.2 for applicants under 25 beyond the oracle's own gap. Version 0.7.0 also adds a language-model proposer (proposer llm.py) with a response cache keyed by SHA-256 for exact replay. In a pilot of 15 runs (mid severity, 5 seeds; Claude Haiku 4.5 as proposer, model version and temperature not pinned, reproducible from the released cache) both loops ended at the correct harness, but without the gate 13 admissions were harmful and missed flags during adaptation reached 22.3 percent in the scope family, against 0 and 2.0 percent with the gate.

evidence_items.summary: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).
evidence_items.title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are becoming central to GeoAI systems, yet their evaluation rarely considers the elicitation of geospatial data requirements. This omission is critical as retrieval oriented geo-analytic tasks cannot be supported reliably without first identifying the necessary datasets and constraints. GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark for assessing whether LLMs can infer the datasets, the supporting resources and the constraints required by geo-analytic requests in natural language. The benchmark is structured around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, reflecting long-standing challenges in geospatial information retrieval and related natural language tasks. Ground truth requirements are encoded in a fixed, provider-independent schema for reproducible evaluation of resource identification and attribute-level specification. Experiments on seven models under minimal prompting indicate that identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with GPT-5.4 Thinking achieving the best result by recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of benchmark requests. Results further indicate that accurate fitness-for-use specification remains more difficult as inferential demands increase.
evidence_items.title: GeoFitBench-LLM: A Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Capabilities in Geospatial Data Requirements Elicitation for Geo-Analytic Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Agricultural visual models are typically evaluated for either recognition or localization, but reliable diagnosis requires identifying what is present and localizing the evidence. Agricultural visual question answering (VQA) datasets carry rich semantic labels but rarely link them to image regions, and adding such annotations by hand is costly at scale. We introduce AgroGround, a large-scale dataset for grounded agricultural recognition: identifying plant diseases and other agricultural targets and localizing their image regions. An automated pipeline converts the labels of eight agricultural VQA datasets into annotations for disease lesions and whole objects, producing 794,850 instruction examples. Healthy images provide negative supervision for disease queries, teaching the model to return empty predictions. We fine-tune a shared vision-language model on known-target grounding instructions combined with instructions requiring both recognition and localization. We evaluate predicted identities, regions, joint correctness, and healthy-image abstention on 1,480 human-verified images disjoint from all training data. Grounding-only fine-tuning reduces recognition accuracy from 51.8\% to 29.1\%, while adding recognition-and-localization instructions raises it to 72.6\%. With images and annotations held fixed, combining the two formats raises joint accuracy from 19.2\% to 43.3\% at comparable grounding. Healthy negatives raise abstention on healthy images to 95.0\%, and reinforcement learning improves lesion-level grounding. The resulting 2B model exceeds its annotation teacher in grounding F1 on our benchmark and on the external PlantSeg test set. AgroGround establishes a benchmark for grounded agricultural recognition, measuring joint correctness of identity and localization along with abstention on healthy images. The code is available at https://github.com/AB-Abdulla/AgroGround.
evidence_items.title: AgroGround: Multi-Granularity Grounded Recognition in Agriculture

evidence_items.summary: In this paper, we study physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation---moving the goal from reproducing how objects look to capturing how they move and function. Inspired by the literature on procedural and agentic generation, we present Artisan, a system that extends the latest method Articraft by introducing a multi-agent pipeline with physical simulation feedback, enabling comprehensive attributes beyond geometry, appearance, and physically plausible articulation, such as collision-free motion, stability under gravity, and accurate mass and material properties. Furthermore, we construct a unified benchmark spanning four key aspects: spatial fidelity, physical plausibility, downstream task performance, and overall quality. The benchmark encompasses 100 reference assets from ArtVIP and LightWheel, 50 stability prompts, and 50 ABO objects with reference masses, with protocols evaluating various metrics. Through extensive evaluation of more than 10 representative models, Artisan achieves competitive spatial fidelity while attaining the lowest collision rates and highest stability rates among the evaluated methods. Together, our system and benchmark establish insights for advancing 3D generation towards physically plausible, functionally usable assets.
evidence_items.title: Towards Physically Grounded Articulated 3D Assets: A Multi-Agent Pipeline and Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Open-ended questions are commonly used in survey research to supplement closed-ended questions by capturing respondents’ views, reasons, and priorities in their own words. However, coding these responses for analysis remains time-consuming and difficult to standardise. Recent advances in automated coding, especially through large language models (LLMs), have renewed interest in using open-ended responses at scale, but their evaluation is often difficult and framed mainly in terms of classification accuracy and agreement with human coding. This paper develops a Total Survey Error framework for evaluating automated coding of open-ended survey responses as part of survey measurement and data production. Model outputs are assessed using existing human-coded data as a high-quality operational benchmark, with the evaluation examining six complementary dimensions, such as processing agreement, measurement validity, prevalence distortion, coding density, response-form sensitivity, and operational reliability. The framework is applied to data using open-ended survey responses from the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen). The paper aims to inform how automated coding systems, including LLMs, can be assessed in practice, and what issues survey researchers should consider when evaluating their suitability for open-ended survey coding, and how improved coding may enable wider use of open-ended questions in large-scale quantitative surveys.Keywords: automated coding; large language models; measurement validity; open-ended survey responses; survey data quality; Total Survey Error
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) for Coding Open-Ended Survey Responses: A Total Survey Error Framework

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid deployment of AI-native applications in complex wellbore operations requires unified, high-quality data integration to sustain continuous model evolution and reliable asset lifecycle management. However, heterogeneity in standards, semantics, and system architectures across legacy operational datasets limits their immediate applicability for dynamic and agile AI workflows. In alignment with the digital transformation priorities on information management, knowledge integration, and emerging technology implementations, this study develops a Human- and Entity-Centric Agentic Travelling Approach (HATA) for constructing dynamic-static ontology that support adaptive, cross-scenario data integration. This supports the energy transformation by enabling adaptive data integration for complex decision scenarios, validated through 3 typical types of downhole failure cases. HATA introduces a self-organising ontology construction framework composed of three specialised AI agents configured to address data quality challenges in knowledge modelling, and semantic enabled data integration. The planner interprets engineer-determined themes and decomposes them into ontology construction tasks; the traveller explores latent representational spaces to generate ontology candidates optimised for scenario relevance; and the supervisor assesses structural and semantic consistency, providing iterative feedback to guide refinement. The approach was evaluated using operational datasets (2021-2024) from 45 shale-oil wellbores in western China, focusing on wax deposition, scaling, and pump leakage, with corresponding financial management.

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-guided evolutionary optimization has successfully improved prompts, programs, and even entire AI systems. Most optimization methods select a candidate from the search frontier, then mutate it in one LLM pass based only on its failures. This focus on the frontier can stall on production AI systems, where isolated failures reveal little about complex, hidden interactions. We introduce CoCoEvolve (Cortex Code Evolve), an evolutionary optimizer built around what we call meta-reflection, wherein an agentic mutator (Cortex Code) selectively retrieves evidence from the entire evolutionary history and probes the live system before verifying and proposing mutations. We apply CoCoEvolve to optimize three classes of production AI systems: data agents, LLM-powered data pipelines, and data engineering workflows. On DABStep, CoCoEvolve tops the public leaderboard, reaching 92.8% held-out hard accuracy compared to 78.4% for Meta-Harness and 30.4% for GEPA under matched conditions. Across six LLM data pipeline workloads, it outperforms every evaluated baseline. On data-eng-bench, CoCoEvolve lifts test-set solve rate from 59.1% to 77.4%, past the best baseline of 73.6%. It also has 11 percentage points higher accuracy than GEPA on HotpotQA while remaining competitive with specialized optimizers on established mathematical and systems benchmarks. Matched ablations confirm that each component of CoCoEvolve contributes to these gains, demonstrating the value of meta-reflection for optimizing production AI systems.
evidence_items.title: Meta-Reflective Evolution Effectively Improves Production AI Systems

evidence_items.summary: Recent AI systems have achieved strong results on a wide range of benchmarks, yet these gains have not translated into economically meaningful deployment across many professional domains. We argue that this gap is largely an evaluation problem: widely used benchmarks lack sustained performance measurement on real and economically valuable workflows. This paper introduces Agents' Last Exam (ALE), a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on long horizon, economically valuable, real world tasks with verifiable outcomes. Developed in collaboration with 250+ industry experts, ALE covers non-physical industries defined with reference to O*NET / SOC 2018 (the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy). It is organized around a task taxonomy with 55 sub fields grouped into 13 industry clusters covering 1K+ tasks. Current results show that the hardest tier remains far from saturated: across mainstream harness and backbone configurations, the average full pass rate is below 1%. ALE is designed as a living benchmark: its task pool grows continuously as new workflows and industries are onboarded. More broadly, ALE is intended not merely as another leaderboard, but as an instrument for closing the gap between benchmark success and GDP relevant impact.
evidence_items.title: Agents' Last Exam

evidence_items.summary: We combine GeneNetwork's 1TB structured database with its metadata as an RDF graph and an associated literature corpus. We benchmark frontier and local LLMs querying it through four architectures: document, graph and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of the three. We evaluate them on 40 domain specific expert-curated questions with a new metric: the satisfaction frequency psi (psi, i.e, the share of questions answered with precision and recall of at least 70% or an f1 of at least 60%). psi ranks systems the same way precision, recall and f1 -- a machine learning metric built from the harmonic mean of precision and recall -- but is easier to read and assess for humans. System architecture had a large effect: with full use of Claude Opus 4.8 the plain document RAG of our earlier GNQA system had a psi of 36% against 86% for our new combined tools. Delegating most of the work from Claude Opus 4.8 to a local model halved query costs while still reaching a psi of 59%.

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used both as recommenders and to explain recommendations, yet producing faithful, user-centric explanations and evaluating them rigorously remain open problems, compounded by a documented reproducibility crisis in recommender systems research. In this work we formalise recommendation as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process and propose a unified, three-tier agentic framework that couples a simulation environment (RecoWorld), a reproducible policy engine (RecBole), and a cognitive LLM user agent. As an offline, single-turn validation of this framework on the MovieLens-32M dataset, we benchmark preliminary single-epoch checkpoints of traditional policies (Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR), Convolutional Neural Collaborative Filtering and Neural Matrix Factorisation (NeuMF)), generate LLM-based explanations from the BPR recommendations and score them with quantitative diversity, faithfulness, counterfactual and readability metrics over roughly one million user-item pairs, and run an LLM-as-user interview simulation in which explanations produced by a Qwen2.5 explainer are assessed by a Llama-3 respondent through a six-criterion explanation-quality survey; a controlled comparison on 2000 users shows that replacing BPR with the more accurate NeuMF policy leaves these survey scores practically unchanged. The generated explanations prove highly faithful (feature precision 0.9996, sufficiency 0.9999) and user-tailored explanations (unique-sentence ratio 0.9978), and simulated users rate clarity highest (3.86/5) yet trust lowest (2.60/5). Faithful template explanations are, therefore, trusted less than they are understood, motivating a shift towards controllable generative explanation and scalable simulated evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Simulating Users to Evaluate LLM-Generated Explanations in Recommender Systems: A Unified Agentic Framework and Empirical Study with Preliminary Results

evidence_items.summary: Tool-use language agents are evaluated on benchmarks that assume clean inputs, unambiguous tool registries, and reliable APIs. Real deployments violate all these assumptions: user typos propagate into hallucinated tool names, a misconfigured request timeout can stall an agent indefinitely, and duplicate tool names across servers can freeze an SDK. We study these failures as a sim-to-real gap in the tool-use partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where deployment noise enters through the observation, action space, reward-relevant metadata, or transition dynamics. We introduce RobustBench-TC, a benchmark with 22 perturbation types organized by these four POMDP components, each grounded in a verified GitHub issue or documented tool-calling failure. Across 21 models from 1.5B to 32B parameters (including the closed-source o4-mini), the robustness profile is sharply uneven: observation perturbations reduce accuracy by less than 5%, while reward-relevant and transition perturbations reduce accuracy by roughly 40% and 30%, respectively; scale alone does not close these gaps. We then propose ToolRL-DR, a domain-randomization reinforcement learning (RL) recipe that trains a tool-use agent on perturbation-augmented trajectories spanning the three statically encodable POMDP components. On a 3B backbone, ToolRL-DR-Full retains roughly three-quarters of clean accuracy and reaches an aggregate perturbed accuracy comparable to open-source 14B function-calling baselines while substantially narrowing the gap to o4-mini. It closes approximately 27% of the Transition gap despite never seeing transition perturbations in training, suggesting that RL on adversarial static tool-use inputs induces a more persistent retry policy that transfers to unseen runtime failures. The dataset, code and benchmark leaderboard are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: When Simulation Lies: A Sim-to-Real Benchmark and Domain-Randomized RL Recipe for Tool-Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Detecting communicative meaning in dialogue requires modeling not only lexical content but also the participant-role structures through which sentiment, emotion, politeness, and formality (SEPF) are expressed. Existing approaches rely on contextual language representations while leaving semantic roles implicit. We introduce a role-aware transformer architecture that maps the four SEPF dimensions to theory-grounded Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) configurations, incorporating these configurations directly into the transformer's self-attention mechanism. Role-aware attention models non-directional internal states (sentiment and emotion), while directional role-aware attention captures initiator-to-recipient relations for external cues (politeness and formality). The resulting role-aware representations are fused with contextual embeddings through a learned gate that adaptively weights how much role information each input contributes, rather than appending semantic roles as an auxiliary feature vector. Across four benchmark datasets, the framework yields statistically reliable gains over strong BERT-based baselines for emotion, politeness, and formality, with gains concentrated in theoretically predicted cases such as low-frequency, complex emotions and highly polite expressions; sentiment improvements are marginal and non-significant, suggesting that sentiment is conveyed more through lexical choice than participant-role structure. Additional evaluation on real-world data demonstrates that the framework improves both predictive performance and model traceability. These results demonstrate that linguistically grounded modifications to transformer self-attention improve the detection of communicative meaning, generalize beyond benchmark datasets to real-world mental-health data, and yield traceable, role-grounded explanations that extend beyond predictive performance to interpretability.
evidence_items.title: REFLECT: Role-Aware Detection of Sentiment, Emotion, Politeness, and Formality

evidence_items.summary: With the advances of coding agents, software developers are spending more time reviewing code than writing code. As human review velocity falls behind agentic code generation, it is tempting to build automated review agents towards a future of "lights-off" software factory with little to no human supervision. To assess the practicality of such a fully autonomous software factory, we construct CRBugBench, a new benchmark that evaluates whether review agents detect human-verified bugs. We build a data pipeline that mines bugs from repository history, and pair each bug with its introducing PR to form a review task. CRBugBench consists of 1,000 review tasks across 98 open-source GitHub repositories, and 800 additional tasks from proprietary industry repositories at one large company. We then use the benchmark to study agent review quality: We found that SOTA review agents do well: the best (claude-opus-5 with copilot-cli) catches 71.9% of bugs within its top-5 comments, up from 47.7% (opus-4.6) in five months of model evolution. Yet agents remain less effective on complex changes and bugs requiring non-local reasoning, with sharp performance drops on proprietary industry repositories where project context is more often needed. To improve bug detection, we found scaling compute helps most through prompt changes: exploration-nudging prompts gain up to 5.8% performance at 10% higher cost. From these findings, we derive concrete guidance for developers to adopt review agents - scaling review effort to PR complexity, steering agents by project priorities, supplying repository knowledge, dispatching models by PR characteristics, and monitoring quality as models evolve.
evidence_items.title: (When) Should a Software Factory be Lights-off? Benchmarking Code Review Agents on Bug Detection

evidence_items.summary: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. When looking at the scientific literature to determine which feature selection method to use, practitioners across domains face an unrepresentative landscape of benchmarking. Despite extensive research, existing feature selection benchmarks provide limited guidance because they rely on outdated models, ad hoc evaluation protocols, or artificially generated data that do not reflect real-world problems. To close the gap between scientific benchmarking and real-world applications, we introduce SelectArena, a modern benchmark for feature selection. We compare 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets, covering classification and regression problems, using standardized evaluation protocols and state-of-the-art tabular (foundation) models. Our results reveal clear trade-offs across predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. Tree-based methods, CART and RFImportance, along with F-Test are Pareto-optimal when taking into account predictive performance and runtime. F-Test, information-theory-, and distance-based methods lead on stability and validity, with F-Test emerging as a balanced choice across our metrics. Search-based methods are slow, unstable and achieve low performance. SelectArena turns these findings into practical guidance and, as an extensible platform, supports future feature selection research.
evidence_items.title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data

evidence_items.summary: Professional agents increasingly work through command-line interfaces and multiple tools over shared workspaces containing files, messages, and business applications. These environments create safety risks that are difficult to capture with attacks placed at a single, known read location. We introduce APEX-Harm, a benchmark for evaluating prompt and script injection against long-horizon agents performing finance, consulting, and legal tasks in large workspaces. Each task contains 115 to 328 files, together with email, calendar, chat, document, spreadsheet, PDF, and code-execution tools exposed through MCP servers. The benchmark includes six attack categories covering static and dynamic injections, task-specific script replacement, and attacker-provided generic scripts, and evaluates attack success, exposure, and task performance. We evaluate 12 frontier models on 180 task instances per model. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 have the lowest overall attack success rates (8% and 20%), while task-specific script replacement and attacker-provided generic script attacks remain substantially more effective, averaging 81-84% and 73% attack success, respectively. Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves the highest mean task score (0.877) while still exhibiting a 33% attack success rate. These results show that completing the requested task is not sufficient evidence of safe behavior: an agent can produce a correct deliverable while also performing an unauthorized action in the workspace.
evidence_items.title: APEX-Harm: Evaluating Agent Safety in Shared Professional Workspaces

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.
evidence_items.title: MAGMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Embodied Agents under Dynamic Tasks and Execution Failures

evidence_items.summary: Agentic orchestration delegates tasks to sub-agents with independent contexts, providing a key path to extending the effective execution horizon of large language model agents. However, existing orchestration methods face two limitations: in execution, current methods fix sub-agents' goals and harnesses at creation time, limiting their adaptability to dynamic real-world environments; in optimization, sparse and delayed feedback constrains effective learning of the orchestration policy. To address these limitations, we introduce POrchestra, an on-the-fly proactive agentic orchestration framework. It allows sub-agents to proactively communicate with the orchestrator at any logical point to request harness adjustments while maintaining continuity of local execution. This mechanism not only enables sub-agents to adapt seamlessly to dynamic environments but also naturally inspires On-Policy Orchestration Distillation (OPOD) based on hindsight feedback. OPOD attributes sub-agents' proactive revision requests back to preceding orchestration decisions to derive targeted improvement signals, and leverages these signals as process supervision alongside the final reward to optimize the orchestration policy. We evaluate POrchestra on three long-horizon agent benchmarks spanning deep research, dynamic digital assistance, and software engineering. POrchestra improves task success by an average of 9.1% relative to the strongest baseline; combined with OPOD, it improves small-orchestrator success by an average of 10.0% relative to existing training baselines. POrchestra also achieves a more favorable cost-performance trade-off. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/XueyangFeng/POrchestra.
evidence_items.title: Proactive Agentic Orchestration

evidence_items.summary: As the production of software passes into the hands of software itself, coding agents are increasingly commissioned to build agents fitted to their users' own workflows. This delegation carries a quiet assumption, that the delivered agent will faithfully serve the requirement it was built for, rather than merely appear to. No existing benchmark tests that assumption. We introduce AgentSWE, a benchmark for agent software engineering spanning three stages of the agent development lifecycle: Creation of a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, Editing of production agent codebases, and Optimization toward a measurable target. Each of its 25 tasks is framed as a commission rather than an exam: the builder iterates against a handful of illustrative cases, while acceptance exercises the frozen submission on held-out cases designed to span the full requirement, grading behavior against requirement-derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates or, for Optimization, against the source benchmark's own objective. Evaluating a range of coding agents across models and harnesses, we find that none comes close to delivering what a requirement asks for: the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm, not the corner case. An accompanying empirical analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring failure modes, among them overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion, each a signal by which coding agents can learn to build the agents they are asked for.
evidence_items.title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?

evidence_items.summary: Satirical news is a unique form of misinformation: it is intended to be humorous by the original publication source but can be misinterpreted. Explanation of satirical news articles is challenging because recent and local context needs to be incorporated. This is a pilot study that explores explanation generation for satirical news articles from Australia and compares them alongside those from USA. The paper demonstrates that framing explanations on unreliable narrator theory on open-weights models can be a feasible, cost-effective alternative to frontier models. We find that models identify the satirical tropes more accurately on the American source than the Australian one. This work results in a novel dataset and an evaluation benchmark for satirical explanation.
evidence_items.title: Unreliable Narrator Framing as a Cost-effective Mechanism for Satire Explanation of Australian and American Satirical News

evidence_items.summary: Web agents increasingly browse, interpret, and act on web content on behalf of users. In many realistic workflows, however, the visual evidence they consume is not neutral: charts and dashboards can be misleading, shaping judgments without issuing any explicit malicious instruction. Unlike chart question answering, Web Agents treat charts as intermediate evidence whose misinterpretation can propagate into concrete downstream actions --- a reliability risk that remains underexplored. We introduce MisVisAgentBench, the first paired executable benchmark for evaluating how misleading visualizations affect Web Agent execution. It comprises 280 task instances in matched clean--misleading pairs that differ only in chart evidence. We further provide a diagnostic framework that isolates misleading-induced failures from baseline task difficulty (Zhu et al., 2025) and captures execution-level effects such as extra browsing steps and decision hesitation. Across thirteen vision-language Web Agents, replacing clean charts with misleading counterparts reduces the average task success rate by more than 34 percentage points. Moreover, these failures predominantly follow the targeted misleading action branch, suggesting that deceptive charts systematically redirect rather than randomly disrupt agent decisions. These results reveal that visualization robustness is a critical yet understudied dimension of Web Agent safety and reliability.
evidence_items.title: When Charts Deceive Web Agents: A Paired Benchmark for Misleading Visualization-Grounded Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports constitute a rich source of expert knowledge and have increasing value in the current political climate, but their heterogeneity and analytical complexity pose challenges for retrieval-augmented question answering. We introduce a benchmark for grounded question answering over 415 open-source geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports, comprising 5,525 document-grounded question-answer pairs spanning factual, inferential, comparative, and risk-oriented questions. We propose a document-aware generation pipeline that profiles reports before generating questions and validate dataset quality through expert annotation and an LLM-as-judge protocol. Using the benchmark, we evaluate 15 retrieval systems and six open-weight LLMs for RAG. We find that models perform similarly on document-level retrieval, while at the harder chunk level retrieval quality is not driven by embedding-model scale: bge-m3, a mid-size open encoder matches an order of magnitude larger ones and outperforms commercial embedding APIs. In contrast, answer generation remains challenging even given the gold evidence, particularly for inferential and risk-oriented questions.
evidence_items.title: GeopoliticalQA: Benchmarking Retrieval and Generation over Intelligence Reports

evidence_items.summary: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. evidence_items.summary: SWE-Bench Pro has emerged as a standard benchmark for evaluating software engineering agents on challenging repository-level tasks. However, our analysis work show that its evaluation is undermined by two sources of unreliability: reward hacking, enabled by leakage of gold solutions or hidden evaluation information, and task quality issues, including misleading problem statements and improperly scoped tests. These issues can inflate benchmark performance and obscure agents' true coding ability. We present SWE-Bench Pro Verified, a verified version of SWE-Bench Pro that addresses both problems. Our approach combines anti-hacking safeguards that eliminate major leakage channels without disrupting normal agent functionality, with task refinement that minimally corrects inconsistencies within flawed instances. Evaluations on SWE-Bench Pro Verified reveal that some models perform substantially worse than previously evaluated, suggesting that existing results on SWE-Bench Pro may overestimate real software engineering capability. SWE-Bench Pro Verified offers a more trustworthy benchmark for assessing software engineering agents.

Native application environments require substantial construction and integration effort, which limits application coverage and increases the risk of application-specific overfitting. evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly being deployed in governmental settings, yet few existing evaluation frameworks jointly reflect the values of public administration and the linguistic requirements of non-English contexts. We present the Grip on LLMs framework, a systematic evaluation suite for Dutch governmental use developed in collaboration with domain experts from a major Dutch municipal organisation. Through an advisory board process, user research, and a survey of the users of civil-servant chatbot, we identify six evaluation dimensions (factuality, honesty, social bias, energy consumption, cost, and training data transparency) and operationalise them into a benchmark suite covering more than 30 multilingual and Dutch-specific models. Our results reveal that no single model excels across all dimensions, and that trade-offs are unavoidable: higher quality consistently comes at greater environmental impact and financial cost, while bias remains largely independent of both. We further find that factuality (whether a model answers correctly) and honesty (whether a model acknowledges what it does not know) are governed by distinct properties, with high factuality not implying high honesty. To make these findings actionable for non-technical audiences, we release a publicly accessible, user-friendly model overview designed for the full range of stakeholders involved in governmental LLM selection, from engineers to policymakers.
evidence_items.title: From Values to Benchmarks: Evaluating Large Language Models for Governmental Use in Dutch

evidence_items.summary: AI agents built on large language models can assist not only legitimate tasks but also relational manipulation. AI agents can be used to help a user maintain a deceptive identity, intensify emotional dependency, isolate a target, or prepare for later extraction. We conceptualise this risk as agentic relationship harm: workflow-level assistance that can exploit recipient vulnerability, persuasive influence, and relational power asymmetry. Existing safety evaluations and generic guardrails often treat harmfulness as a property of isolated outputs, missing role-sensitive interaction patterns. To study this, we introduce a 110-prompt benchmark with balanced attacker-and victim-side cases, a relationship-specific labelling framework, and a lightweight post-generation policy gate for local agent deployments. In our evaluation, the relationship-specific gate outperforms generic safety prompting under automated judging, with no harmful-compliance cases identified on the main benchmark or multi-turn stress test while preserving victim-side protective intervention. These results suggest that relationship harm is a distinct sociotechnical risk surface and that role-sensitive evaluation plus lightweight policy gating offers a practical path beyond generic refusal prompting.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Relationship Harm: Benchmarking and Gating Relational Manipulation in AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: When an operator’s instruction conflicts with a codified safety rule, an assistant should recognize the conflict and defer to the rule. This is a pragmatic problem with an objective answer: the correct action follows from a published regulation, while the difficulty is linguistic. Existing evaluations do not target this case: general safety benchmarks ask whether a model emits harmful content, instruction-following suites score obedience to formatting constraints, and work on sycophancy and rule-following shows that models can be argued out of a stated rule, but none set a user’s authoritative instruction against an external, codified rule whose deferral is objectively correct. This paper introduces a benchmark of 75 items (60 rule conflicts, 15 no-conflict controls) grounded in the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs) and in paraphrased International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) procedures, spanning four conflict framings, each presented with and without the governing rule and followed by a pushback turn. Eleven instruction-tuned models were evaluated across 1649 responses and scored by an independent language model judge (second judge Cohen’s kappa = 0.84). Because the items are author-constructed and now validated by two independent domain reviewers, compliance rates are reported as measurements on a validated benchmark rather than as mere rankings, though they remain bounded by the text scenario setting, and the model-scaling results in particular are treated as exploratory. Both model size and alignment were associated with unsafe compliance: within one family compliance fell overall from 0.51 at 0.5B to near zero at 14B, though not strictly monotonically, and at a fixed 7B size a less safety-tuned model complied far more than its aligned peers.
evidence_items.title: Literal to a Fault? How Large Language Models Handle Instructions That Break Codified Operational Rules

evidence_items.summary: The global myopia epidemic, especially among children, poses a major public health burden. Orthokeratology (OK) is an established intervention for slowing myopia progression, yet its conventional practice is constrained by variable treatment responses, an experience-dependent fitting process, and the need for vigilant long-term safety monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers an approach to enhance precision, efficiency, and accessibility across the entire OK care cycle. This review assesses AI applications in OK, encompassing pre-treatment efficacy prediction, AI-assisted lens fitting and automated fit assessment during treatment, and post-treatment safety monitoring with complication risk alert. Evidence indicates that AI models perform comparably to, and in some tasks surpass, human experts in predicting outcomes and determining optimal lens parameters. However, translation from research to routine practice is hindered by limited data quality and diversity, the opacity of complex algorithms, insufficient external validation, and unresolved ethical concerns. Progress depends on building large-scale, diverse datasets, developing interpretable and robust models, and fostering effective human-AI collaboration.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for full-cycle clinical management in orthokeratology: a comprehensive review

evidence_items.summary: System One models output calibrated probabilities over typed answers such as categorical choices, ordinal levels, or binary outcomes, via a non-generative interface. Software can act on these probabilities through thresholds, cost-weighted choices, and escalation rules. Consequently, if these probabilities are miscalibrated or wording-sensitive, the software ma take unintended actions leaving human operators with no textual rationale to inspect. Current evaluations largely report accuracy and calibration on public classification datasets without a clear reference. We present TypedBench, a benchmark for typed decision models like Jev built from seven policy-labelled generators and nine evaluation suites. We report accuracy as median and range across paraphrases, and calibration error relative to the finite-sample noise floor of a matched, perfectly calibrated predictor. We assess probability quality through selective prediction, ordinal proper scoring rules, and realised cost under asymmetric cost matrices. We evaluate a hosted model, an open encoder, and a family of open decoders spanning 0.8B-9B parameters on identical items. The hosted model follows the stated policy but is wording-sensitive and systematically underconfident; under asymmetric costs, using its probabilities can be worse than taking its top answer. Decoders route exactly and are slow as options or questions are added. The decoder is least accurate on policy questions and degrades with more options. Overall, typed decision models must be evaluated jointly on policy adherence, wording robustness, probability quality, and induced decision outcomes.
evidence_items.title: TypedBench: A Benchmark for Calibration, Framing Sensitivity, and Cost in System One Decision Models

evidence_items.summary: Constraint Acquisition (CA) and related research on the validation and enhancement of Mathematical Programming (MP) models using domain knowledge artifacts are currently limited by inadequate benchmarks. The existing benchmarks are loosely organized, provide inconsistent types and formats of artifacts for individual problems, are designed for benchmarking solvers rather than CA algorithms, include narrow classes of problems, or omit crucial details for the reproducibility of experiments and fair comparison of CA methods. We develop a benchmark dataset, a supporting software package, and a benchmarking tool crafted for the consistent, systematic, and comprehensive assessment of CA algorithms, bridging the gap in algorithmic development and experimental infrastructure. This work presents MPMMine, a benchmark suite designed to assess algorithms that discover, validate, and enhance MP models using diverse artifacts. The development of MPMMine is guided by design rules supporting consistency, standardization, completeness, extensibility, openness, and version control. It adopts a uniform structure and relies on open formats. It provides alternative formulations of MP models per problem, tens of parameter instantiations per MP model, and thousands of exemplary solutions and non-solutions in discrete, continuous, and mixed domains, alongside natural-language descriptions to support text-to-model methods. The mpmmine-py Python package provides an application programming interface for accessing the dataset artifacts. The MPMMine Leaderboard is a~tool that systematically evaluates existing CA algorithms using MPMMine under consistent conditions. It leverages open source implementations, runs them in isolated containers adapting input/output to their needs to build an extensive, interactive scoreboard.
evidence_items.title: MPMMine: Better Benchmarks for Constraint Acquisition

evidence_items.summary: Negative polarity items (NPIs), such as "anymore" and "ever", are grammatical only in select environments, predominantly in the context of negation. Because their grammaticality depends on both syntax and semantics, they have a rich, multilingual literature in theoretical linguistics, yet work on NPIs in language models is almost entirely confined to English. We introduce BLiMPPI, a multilingual evaluation suite of over 12,000 NPI minimal pairs in 33 languages, built by a pipeline that discovers NPIs in Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks, labels their licensing environments, and perturbs these into minimal pairs. Evaluating 12 multilingual and 2 monolingual models alongside n-gram baselines, we find that multilingual models struggle most with lower-resource languages and with pairs that are not n-gram solvable. We further examine the effects of NPI typology, language family, licensing variability, and NPI-licenser distance. Data: https://github.com/arzuburcuguven/blimppi-data
evidence_items.title: BLiMPPI: Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for Polarity Items

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. Writing the missing know-how into the agent's prompt makes the prompt long and identical for every input, although different inputs need different guidance. We propose to learn to generate this guidance instead. A small advisor model reads each input and writes structured advice, which is appended to the prompt of a frozen executor. The advisor is trained with hindsight, following work on distillation with privileged information. On a training pool with graded answers, we analyse the executor's failures, run it under several strategies to see which one worked on each input, and let a teacher that sees the grades and the traces write the advice that would have helped. The advisor then learns, by supervised fine-tuning, to write that advice from the input alone. Because the student is a separate small model rather than the executor, it is cheap to train and adds little latency. We call this approach hindsight structured advice distillation (HSAD). On FrontierFinance, a public benchmark of expert-written financial research queries, an 8B advisor raises the qualification rate of Samaya's proprietary research agent, which already leads the benchmark's leaderboard, from 52.9% to 56.6%. This is above the agent's own high-effort configuration, at 37% lower cost per query. We study the generalization of the proposed approach, and in particular show that HSAD also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL and ExpertLongBench.
evidence_items.title: Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics

evidence_items.summary: When an off-the-shelf coding agent is used directly as a robot policy, observing a browser-based 3D interface through screenshots and acting by posing a virtual target gripper through a few tools, the agent's harness, its prompts, tools, and control rules, largely determines success, and until now it has been written by hand. We show that this harness can be improved automatically by another coding agent, the optimizer agent, and report two findings about what makes it work. First, the number of rollouts the optimizer agent sees per round governs whether the evolved harness generalizes: with rounds fixed, held-out success rises as the training batch grows from 5 to 100 rollouts, while small batches overfit the training tasks. Second, the optimizer agent must not be given free rein. Accepting every revision it proposes degrades the harness within a few rounds; a simple Champion-Challenger rule that promotes a revision only if it beats the incumbent on the same fixed cases turns the same loop into one that raises held-out success on LIBERO tasks from 51% to 67% over 30 rounds. Combining the evolved harness with a pretrained policy, through one tool that hands it control, reaches 71.2% on the RoboCasa365 leaderboard benchmark, 13.1 points above the best published entry. Automatic harness evolution for visual-interface robot agents is thus feasible, but its gains hinge on the rollout scale behind each decision and on how the optimizer agent's revisions are selected.
evidence_items.title: Scale and Selection: What Makes Automatic Harness Evolution Work for Visual-Interface Robot Agents

evidence_items.summary: Despite rapid AI adoption in education, rigorous evaluation of AI-powered educational (AIED) systems remains critically underdeveloped, particularly in second-language (L2) education, one of the most common yet least evaluated AI applications. We introduce L2-Bench, an open-source benchmark of 1,000+ task-response pairs to aid the pedagogy-led evaluation of LLM capabilities relating to language learning and assessment. Crucially, L2-Bench measures model performativity on the application of learning experience design principles rather than mere knowledge of those principles or broad learning outcomes. Our contributions include: (1) a validated taxonomy of 12 competencies and 31 subcompetencies validated by 200+ expert practitioners (task authenticity = 4.42/5.00, criteria adequacy = 4.18/5.00); (2) a rubric-based evaluation methodology that we believe can, if adapted, generalize to similar (open-ended, qualitative) disciplines; (3) an evaluation dataset that produces reliable signal about model strengths, weaknesses, and contextual robustness across diverse L2 education scenarios. We find that, among large models, Claude Opus 4.7 performs best overall (85.5%), though is marginally outperformed on several constituent tasks. We also find that performance drops notably on harder tasks (ranging from 69.9%–73.4%). L2-Bench provides education stakeholders better methods to make more informed decisions about real-world AIED adoption, use, and governance, while advancing the maturing science of AI evaluations for education.
evidence_items.title: L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education (Extended Abstract)

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark suites assess model capability on controlled tasks; large-scale conversation corpora capture naturalistic use without user feedback; and in-interface feedback mechanisms record satisfaction without task purpose. Together, they leave a critical gap in LLM evaluation: no existing infrastructure routinely links interaction trajectories to user-defined outcomes. We introduce MonitrLLM, open-source infrastructure for community-centered LLM evaluations that links full conversation transcripts to user-reported task intent and outcome assessments, treating all three as primary evaluative signals rather than optional metadata. To demonstrate the value of this approach, we conducted a two-week feasibility pilot with 26 college students using ChatGPT, collecting 206 evaluation reports with full conversation transcripts. The findings from our pilot demonstrate the value of connecting conversation trajectories with user-reported outcomes. For instance, despite reporting high average satisfaction (4.19/5) with their LLM interactions, participants also experience a substantial 23.1% failure rate on their goal tasks. We also find that multi-turn conversations are reported as failing at 2.5 times the rate of single-turn exchanges, a pattern that reframes extended interaction as a signal of difficulty rather than engagement. We conclude by discussing the value of incorporating direct user feedback with observational data for robust LLM evaluations, and the possibilities for infrastructure that enables this goal.
evidence_items.title: MonitrLLM: A Community-Centered Evaluation Infrastructure for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Sixth generation (6G) networks require intelligent and privacy-preserving solutions to handle traffic complexity, resource allocation, and security challenges. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer advanced reasoning and Federated Artificial Intelligence (FAI) enables distributed learning without directly sharing raw data, their combined application in large-scale network science remains limited. Key issues include non-IID data, decision latency, and limited robustness of centralized models. To address these challenges, this work introduces FALCON-6G (Federated AI and LLM-Oriented Cognitive Optimization in 6G Networks), a novel framework for distributed anomaly detection, traffic prediction, and adaptive resource management. Experiments conducted under federated learning settings with 50 participating clients and 200 global communication rounds on two Open RAN and four intrusion detection datasets show a 22.7% average relative improvement in throughput prediction accuracy and a 17.6% reduction in decision latency compared with FedAvg, along with up to a 23.9% relative improvement in intrusion detection F1-score over FedAvg and a 34.0% reduction in communication overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of FALCON-6G for privacy-aware 6G network optimization. The current evaluation is primarily based on benchmark datasets, and validation in live large-scale 6G/O-RAN environments remains an important direction for future work.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing network science with large language models and federated artificial intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on corpora that contain expressions of human judgment about films, books, music, and more. Yet whether LLMs systematically reproduce evaluative hierarchies remains unclear. Prior research on cultural bias in LLMs suggests competing expectations: models may mirror the popularity signals of internet texts, or may reproduce forms of prestige embedded in critical discourse. We probe this question through a study of film evaluations with eight models from four families (Anthropic, OpenAI, Alibaba, and Mistral), using a 200-film benchmark partitioned into critically acclaimed, commercially successful, and dual-legitimacy (critical acclaim + commercial success) films. Across 20,000 pairwise forced-choice comparisons per model analyzed with Bradley-Terry estimation, we observe a consistent critical acclaim orientation with all models: critically acclaimed yet commercially obscure films are selected over commercially successful yet critically unrecognized ones. This pattern grows with model scale within each family. In addition, nested OLS regression analyses show that evaluative orientation, public visibility, and popular reception distinctly help explain preferences. Adjusting for public visibility reverses the models' preference for dual-legitimacy films over critical acclaim-only films, while additionally accounting for popular reception attenuates much of the disadvantage of films with commercial success only. Finally, evaluative and recommendation-oriented prompt framings produce divergent rankings, suggesting that critical acclaim orientation may manifest indirectly in real-world LLM deployments.
evidence_items.title: Critical Acclaim Orientation in Large Language Models: Evidence from Film Preference Elicitation

evidence_items.summary: Weekly cycles in cyber-threat activity are well documented, but how their timing varies with national weekends is not. Across 384 series from 192 countries, the weekly cycle is nearly universal. In the 43 countries whose weekend we individually sourced, its phase is statistically associated with the local working week. Under the dataset’s date labels, activity is lowest on each country’s own first working day (Sunday) in every Friday–Saturday-weekend country. In just over half of Saturday–Sunday countries, it is lowest one day later (Tuesday rather than Monday). This separation survives any uniform shift of the labels; the absolute weekday depends on an undocumented source timezone. Amplitude is larger under Friday–Saturday weekends (p = 0.0010). Auditing the benchmark, we also found that its ambiguous date format, read with a common parsing idiom, silently discards 59.9% of the data. A full factorial of day-of-week specification, multi-step strategy, and learner, with reimplemented baselines, rolling-origin evaluation, and Diebold–Mariano/Holm inference, shows that specification improves every stable pairing at H = 10 (factors 0.57–0.87) and wins on 190 of 192 countries. It is not sufficient: the multilayer perceptron still loses to a seven-observation moving average. No learned model significantly beats a fixed-window seasonal decomposition at either operational horizon. Accuracy here is governed by specification, not architecture.
evidence_items.title: Weekly Cyber-Threat Seasonality Varies with National Weekend Convention: A Cross-National Forecasting Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Agentic systems increasingly coordinate molecular-design tools, but it is unclear which layer of the stack limits outcomes on real projects. We developed MAGI, an open modular agent that authors objectives, launches and monitors optimization, interprets structure--activity relationships, and revises its strategy accordingly. MAGI generates molecules either directly through the LLM or by delegating to REINVENT 4, with scoring services interchangeable behind a common contract. We tested it across nine retrospective lead-optimization campaigns from three pharmaceutical companies, replayed under fixed temporal cutoffs. Both routes produced valid structures: LLM proposals stayed closer to local chemistry and reached comparable or higher primary activity in fewer operations, whereas REINVENT explored broader chemical space. Whether a campaign met its objective depended on the predictive models, not on the generation route: attainment followed model accuracy on the chemistry proposed, dropping once that chemistry moved outside the model's applicability domain. Separately, a blinded evaluation asked whether the MAGI's output could pass as expert work: chemists were not able to discriminate agentic proposals from held-out compounds, and judged the SAR reasoning broadly plausible yet incomplete. Together, these results position MAGI as a coordination layer pluggable into existing computational chemistry workflows. The ceiling on real projects, however, remains currently set by scorer applicability rather than by tool orchestration.
evidence_items.title: From Benchmark to Bench: Can Agents Survive Real-World Drug Discovery?

evidence_items.summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue systems (FDSDSs) can listen while speaking, enabling natural conversational behaviors such as smooth turn-taking, backchannel handling, and user barge-in handling. However, controlled comparisons of FDSDSs in multi-turn interaction remain challenging, and existing benchmarks offer limited joint coverage of multiple languages, dialogue settings, interaction timing, and response content. We propose M3-DuplexBench, a multi-turn, multilingual, multidomain benchmark for controlled evaluation of FDSDSs. The benchmark jointly evaluates interaction timing and response content in English and Japanese across casual conversation and multi-turn question answering. The English and Japanese question-answering data are derived from a common source corpus, enabling cross-lingual comparisons of timing and content performance. We also provide a reference-conditioned multi-turn setting as an optional diagnostic for examining sensitivity to dialogue history and trajectory mismatch. Experiments with diverse FDSDSs reveal model-specific interaction patterns, differences across languages and domains, and model-dependent effects of dialogue context on both timing and content. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/nttcslab-sp/m3-duplexbench.
evidence_items.title: M3-DuplexBench: A Multi-Turn, Multilingual, Multidomain Benchmark for Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Models

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To enhance the accuracy, interpretability, and robustness of large language models (LLMs) in medical question answering (MedQA). Method: We designed a multi-agent peer-reviewed reasoning method in which multiple LLM agents independently generate chain-of-thought reasoning with candidate answers, then act as peer reviewers to evaluate each other's reasoning for factual correctness and logical soundness. The highest-rated reasoning chain is selected to produce the final answer. Experiments were conducted with five state-of-the-art LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4, DeepSeek-LLM-7B, GPT-oss-20B) on three benchmark datasets: HeadQA, MedQA-USMLE, and PubMedQA. Performance was compared against single-model chain-of-thought reasoning and chain-of-thought-based majority voting. Results: Peer-reviewed reasoning consistently outperformed both baselines. The best model combination achieved an average accuracy of 0.820 across datasets, exceeding the strongest single model (0.777) and majority voting ensembles (up to 0.789). The method also scaled effectively with more participating models, while peer assessments reliably distinguished high- from low-quality reasoning chains. Conclusion: The proposed multi-agent peer-reviewed reasoning method enables LLMs to act as both solvers and evaluators, yielding superior performance in MedQA. By emphasizing reasoning quality rather than answer agreement alone, this approach improves accuracy, interpretability, and robustness, offering a promising direction for trustworthy biomedical AI systems.
evidence_items.title: Let Large Language Models Judge Each Other: Multi-Agent Peer-Reviewed Reasoning for Medical Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: We introduce FactoryBench, a benchmark for evaluating time-series models and LLMs on machine understanding over industrial robotic telemetry. Q&A pairs are organized along four causal levels (state, intervention, counterfactual, decision) instantiating Pearl's ladder of causation, and span five answer formats: four structured formats are scored deterministically and free-form answers are scored by an LLM-as-judge voting protocol. We propose a scalable Q&A generation framework built around structured question templates, present FactoryWave (a dense, multitask, multivariate sensor dataset collected from a UR3 cobot and a KUKA KR10 industrial arm), and construct FactoryBench as a large-scale benchmark of over 70k Q&A items grounded in roughly 15k normalized episodes from FactoryWave, AURSAD, and voraus-AD. Zero-shot evaluation of six frontier LLMs shows that no model exceeds 50% on structured levels or 18% on decision-making, revealing a wide gap between current models and operational machine understanding.
evidence_items.title: FactoryBench: Evaluating Industrial Machine Understanding
