evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.
evidence_items.title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code

evidence_items.summary: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases, exhibiting a 20.0-point gap. Humans attain higher accuracies of 63.4% versus 68.5% for direct and inferential images, respectively, with no significant gap. To locate this failure, we introduce OccludeTrace, a four-stage diagnostic that isolates where the visual reasoning process breaks down. The bottleneck emerges when models must recover the relevant object from the projection within the full image: they succeed on only 50% of failed examples, compared with 91% of examples they answer correctly. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting yield inconsistent improvements and do not reliably eliminate the gap. In contrast, an inpaint-then-confront intervention, which prompts models to first generate a candidate hidden object and then evaluate that hypothesis against the visible physical cue, reduces the gap to a statistically non-significant difference for both models with image-generation capabilities. Together, our results establish a tractable, controlled diagnostic for isolating how VLMs reason about visual content that is missing from an image.
evidence_items.title: OccludeBench: Can VLMs Find What's Missing?

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erd\H{o}s Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. Using Kimi-K3, HOA achieves full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI, and a gold-level score of 97.1% on the IChO. These results closely match the closed-source GPT-5.6 Sol + /Goal baseline on the IMO and IPhO, while exceeding it on the IChO and IOI, demonstrating that systematic feedback can help bridge substantial differences in base-model capability.
evidence_items.title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout the software development lifecycle. This growing reliance on LLMs raises concerns about their trustworthiness, with deception posing a particularly important risk. Deceptive behavior takes the form of misleading responses or assistance in fabricating, concealing, or distorting information. To study this behavior, we introduce SWE-DeceptionBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM deception in software engineering. The benchmark covers six lifecycle stages and two deception triggers: Active Deception, where models recognize infeasible or conflicting requirements but still present them as achievable, and Passive Deception, where models help fulfill explicit user requests to mislead others. We further introduce Neutral, Reward, and Pressure conditions to study the effect of external inducements, resulting in 720 test instances in Chinese and English. Evaluating seven mainstream LLMs, we find substantial deception even under the Neutral condition, with aggregate rates of 49.88% for Active Deception and 64.29% for Passive Deception. Deception rates vary across lifecycle stages, and external inducements affect Active and Passive Deception to different extents. We also evaluate lightweight defenses, finding that guard models miss many deceptive requests, and Self-Reminder reduces but does not eliminate deceptive responses. These findings highlight the need for more effective deception detection and mitigation methods to support trustworthy LLM-based software engineering.
evidence_items.title: SWE-DeceptionBench: Benchmarking Deceptive Behaviors of LLMs Across the Software Development Lifecycle

evidence_items.summary: Stance detection remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) due to implicit opinions, sarcasm, and context-dependent expressions of stance. Although automatic prompt optimization offers an alternative to fine-tuning without updating model parameters, existing structured approaches are not specifically designed around stance-label semantics and class-specific ambiguities. We introduce MoPrO-SD, a stance-specific prompt optimization framework that decomposes prompts into functional semantic modules and refines them sequentially using LLM-based feedback. We study three refinement strategies: instruction-only optimization (I), instruction with reasoning (I+R), and instruction with per-example reasoning (I+R+E), using class-conditioned errors for stance-label refinement. We also introduce VaccineStance, a new human-annotated benchmark for vaccine stance detection. Experiments across four datasets and five open-weight LLMs show that MoPrO-SD improves upon the human-written Base prompt in many settings. On SemEval-2016, class-conditioned feedback achieves higher mean Macro-F1 than pooled feedback for four of five backbones. Both reasoning-based strategies, I+R and I+R+E, achieve strong performance, with their relative effectiveness varying across models and datasets, while remaining competitive with recent prompt optimization methods. The MoPrO-SD code and VaccineStance dataset are available on GitHub.
evidence_items.title: MoPrO-SD: Modular Prompt Optimization for Stance Detection

evidence_items.summary: API specifications serve as critical documentation for modern software development, directly impacting integration efficiency and client code generation. While recent advancements have leveraged Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate initial specifications from source code, existing approaches treat this process as a one-time event - overlooking the needs for continuous validation, long-term maintenance, and market-driven evolution of these artifacts. To address this issue, we present Agent4Spec, an autonomous multi-agent framework featuring two distinct pipelines: (1) a validation pipeline that detects and self-corrects OpenAPI syntax errors, and (2) a market analysis pipeline that conducts competitive research, identifies functional gaps against industry leaders, and automatically generates missing API-spec functionalities. We evaluate Agent4Spec on two curated datasets of API specifications spanning both general-purpose and industrial scenarios. Among 9 SOTA LLMs, the top-performer achieves 100% syntax error detection rates and over 95% implementation success for proposed corrections, while securing over 50% adoption rates for suggested endpoint improvements, representing a practical tool for API development.
evidence_items.title: Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Counterfactual text editing is the ability to revise a given text in light of a hypothetical change while preserving facts not causally affected by that change. When asked what would have happened if a doctor had not recommended surgery, the model output should retain the patient's medical history and modify only the consequences of the decision. This requires causal understanding: a model must determine, without being explicitly instructed to, what events are affected by the hypothetical change and what should remain fixed. This skill is central to human reasoning, especially in safety-critical domains like healthcare or law. By contrast, the task of associational text generation merely generates text statistically associated with the altered condition. In the medical example, an associational response might make the patient's symptoms less severe because milder cases correlate with no surgery. Such responses produce a plausible scenario, but not the counterfactual version of the given one. Prior counterfactual-text datasets do not clearly separate these modes of reasoning. We introduce the Counterfactual Benchmark (CoBe), a testbed for models' zero-shot ability to counterfactually edit a given textual scenario when prompted to do so in a conversationally natural way. CoBe contains 2000 questions spanning healthcare, science and engineering, business, and everyday scenarios. We test a suite of frontier and smaller models, with frontier systems achieving an average score of $58.05\%$. Our findings indicate that models frequently default to associational generation rather than preserving the causal structure of the original scenario. Moreover, performance does not scale consistently with either model size or output token length, suggesting that the failure may reflect model training objectives rather than insufficient model capacity.
evidence_items.title: CoBe: A Benchmark For Conversational Counterfactual Text Editing

evidence_items.summary: As LLMs become increasingly capable of implementing software, a critical bottleneck emerges: whether they truly understand what users want. Users often begin with vague intent, leaving important requirements to be clarified through interaction. In repository-level development, misunderstandings can propagate and cause costly rework. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate implementation from complete specifications or underspecified requests, overlooking pre-coding requirement clarification. Prior clarification studies mainly focus on function-level tasks. It therefore remains unclear how well LLMs can transform vague intent into clear requirements through interaction and how this capability affects subsequent code generation. We introduce ReqClarifyBench, an interactive requirement clarification benchmark for repository-level software development. It contains 341 tasks spanning game, miniapp, and web development, each with a vague user intent, a human-validated requirement document, and code evaluation artifacts. We employ LLM-based user simulators with diverse personas derived from real-world conversations. We evaluate six LLMs in terms of clarification effectiveness and generated requirement document quality. Results show that stronger clarification effectiveness does not necessarily translate into higher document quality, and performance varies substantially across user personas. We also find that coding-agent harnesses do not further improve requirement document quality compared with their base LLMs. These findings offer insights for building LLM-based end-to-end software development systems.
evidence_items.title: Don't Guess, Just Ask: Evaluating Interactive Requirement Clarification for Repository-Level Software Development

evidence_items.summary: We introduce MVGraph, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) on multi-graph reasoning where the evidence required by a query is distributed across multiple interrelated visual graph views. Although such evidence commonly resides in source-specific graphs, temporal snapshots, or local observations, existing graph reasoning benchmarks remain confined to a single self-contained structure, assessing only graph perception and reasoning while leaving the alignment and composition of evidence across views underexplored. MVGraph comprises 8k instances spanning 8 \textit{graph-theoretic} tasks, abstracted from two multi-graph scenarios (partial and temporal graph views). Each problem is programmatically constructed and verified to be unsolvable from a single view. Beyond end-to-end evaluation, we decompose multi-graph reasoning into four complementary capabilities---Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning---and design 29 diagnostic tasks with 64k instances to probe each one, along with golden intermediate representations for evaluating the intermediate process. Across 15 LVLMs, we reveal the difficulty of multi-graph reasoning and identify cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as prominent bottlenecks through stage-oriented diagnostics. Meanwhile, temporal constraints and increasing view counts expose further capability boundaries. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AAAndy-Zhu/MVGraph.
evidence_items.title: MVGraph: Benchmarking LVLMs on Evidence Composition across Multi-View Visual Graph

evidence_items.summary: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.
evidence_items.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation

evidence_items.summary: LLM-generated service-call code is increasingly important for service computing, where developers rely on large language models (LLMs) to compose services and invoke third-party services. However, current approaches have not yet evaluated the invocation and execution of services in the actual code environment. To support execution-grounded evaluation, we present the Service-Call Code Generation Benchmark (SCCGBench), a benchmark of 3,135 traceable and decontamination-filtered RapidAPI call functions from real GitHub repositories. SCCGBench uses redacted-intent generation to reduce circular leakage and introduces Mock, Robust, ParamF1, and host-, endpoint-, method-, and parameter-level diagnostics. Mock denotes a virtual-execution hit that simultaneously matches the gold host, endpoint, and HTTP method, while Robust further requires status checking and exception handling. We evaluate six code LLMs and one non-neural retrieval baseline under intent-only, retrieval-augmented, and gold-documentation Oracle settings. Results show that models often generate syntactically correct or superficially similar HTTP-request code but achieve low Mock success in the intent-only setting; the strongest evaluated model obtains only 3.76% Mock. Under the gold-documentation Oracle settings (C3 and C5), Mock reaches 88.73%--90.52% for the open-source models evaluated in RQ2 and 76.47%--81.86% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, whereas sparse and dense retrieval remain far below this oracle level. The findings indicate that service/API grounding is the main bottleneck: Mock is dominated by host, endpoint, and method alignment, while ParamF1 separately reveals parameter-alignment errors. SCCGBench provides an execution-grounded benchmark for Web service invocation, API recommendation, service-interface retrieval, endpoint grounding, and reliable service-call automation.
evidence_items.title: SCCGBench: Executability-Oriented Evaluation for Real-World Web Service-Call Code Generation

evidence_items.summary: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. We introduce GeoSpatialBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate an escalating progression of spatial cognition, ranging from spatial relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Grounded in real-world urban data across six geographically diverse cities, GeoSpatialBench evaluates a comprehensive taxonomy of 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations across structured GeoJSON and map image modalities, with ground-truth references and constraints verified via GIS operations. Our empirical evaluation across frontier MLLMs uncovers a stark spatial gap: structured GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and while models show reasonable competence on qualitative topological and ordering, performance drops on quantitative metric relations. Crucially, editing performance on ordering relations declines relative to QA, and most failed edits violate at least one specified spatial constraint. These results highlight a gap between passively recognizing spatial relations and actively manipulating geometric configurations. GeoSpatialBench provides an open, rigorous diagnostic testbed to benchmark these spatial limitations, laying essential empirical groundwork for physically grounded world models and embodied spatial AI.
evidence_items.title: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing

evidence_items.summary: Group-based policy optimization has been increasingly used to train large language model (LLM) agents from sparse outcome rewards by comparing trajectories or steps within a group. However, on difficult long-horizon agentic tasks, we found this comparison suffers from a sampling imbalance: repeated or low-effect actions dominate the high-probability region of the policy, leaving useful state-changing actions under-sampled. This imbalance produces many all-failed rollout groups, where the relative advantages within such a group provide no direction for updating the policy. Consequently, the sampling imbalance and the all-failed groups collapse into a self-perpetuating credit trap: failure-dominated sampling yields no learning signal, allowing repeated low-effect actions to persist. To break this trap, we propose Coverage-conditioned Group Policy Optimization (CovGPO), which uses first-visit observation coverage only when all samples in a group receive zero outcome reward. Specifically, within such groups, CovGPO assigns higher relative advantages to state-exploring actions without corrupting the original reward signal, as reaching new observations is a prerequisite for task success. Experiments on two challenging agentic benchmarks, ALFWorld and WebShop, show that CovGPO consistently improves over group-based baselines, with particularly large gains on hard tasks.
evidence_items.title: Learning from All-Failed Groups via First-Visit Coverage in Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks

evidence_items.summary: As AI systems tackle increasingly open-ended research problems, human experts may struggle to assess results and guide further progress. The model itself may be the best available optimizer and evaluator. The challenge is obtaining useful self-supervision within that homogeneous loop, where a model risks reinforcing its own blind spots rather than correcting them. We ask whether a model can learn from the collective intelligence of its own team. Introducing our new paper, Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision : Detailed Blog: https://pub.sakana.ai/mass/ Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12176 Code: https://github.com/SakanaAI/mass We introduce Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS). One shared model solves tasks through a team of virtual subagents, searches for better multi-agent workflows, then uses its own judgments to select the best ones. Training on the best team’s executions distills the team’s collective experience back into the shared model. We ran two cycles using a 27B open-weights model on synthetic open-ended research tasks. After the second cycle, score per output token reached 1.2-1.6x the base model’s level across four research benchmarks. Three key results: MASS enables role generalization within an RSI loop: training only on task-solving data from the optimizee naturally improves the capabilities of both the optimizer and the evaluator. multi-agent trajectories are more efficient training data than single-agent trajectories for RSI. optimizer capacity, rather than evaluator capacity, can be the bottleneck in the speed of improvement. We believe the community needs to investigate homogeneous RSI carefully to support AI safety. When a model is also its own evaluator, shared blind spots could allow mistakes to be accepted as progress and reinforced through training. For AI to improve beyond human expertise safely, we need to understand these failures and preserve effective ways to detect them and intervene.
evidence_items.title: Recursive Self-Improvement through Collective Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) has become a key benchmark for evaluating natural language processing systems, and multiple-choice question answering is widely adopted for assessing reasoning, comprehension, and commonsense inference capabilities. However, traditional embedding-based approaches often struggle with complex reasoning and have limited access to external knowledge. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong language understanding and reasoning abilities, relying on a single model remains challenging because of hallucinations, model biases, and differences in training data, architectures, and domain expertise. Consequently, no single model consistently performs best across diverse multiple-choice question answering tasks. To address these limitations, we propose an ensemble framework for multiple-choice question answering. The framework incorporates a model selection mechanism that identifies model combinations with complementary error patterns to improve the error-correction capability of the ensemble. In addition, when disagreements occur among the selected base models, a Thinking Model is dynamically invoked to resolve conflicting predictions, thereby reserving advanced reasoning for cases requiring additional resolution. We evaluate nine open-source LLMs on five datasets in Chinese and English. Each dataset is partitioned into 30% validation data for model selection and 70% held-out test data for final evaluation, with the experiment independently repeated five times. evidence_items.summary: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. evidence_items.summary: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.

evidence_items.summary: Deepfake detectors are rarely evaluated on Arabic-media content. We introduce Arab-DF, an Arabic-media visual deepfake dataset of 1066 authentic and 11,240 manipulated videos covering four manipulation families. Thirteen public detector checkpoints are evaluated zero-shot under a common protocol, and each must first reproduce its DeepfakeBench Celeb-DF-v2 frame-level AUC within ±0.02; eight meet this criterion. On the fixed 824-video subset, their mean video-level AUC falls from 0.820 on Celeb-DF-v2 to 0.552 on Arab-DF (ΔAUC = −0.267), and five have bootstrap 95% confidence intervals above 0.5. When the authentic sample is enlarged from 75 to 392 while retaining 749 manipulated videos, the mean is 0.508 (95% CI [0.478, 0.537]); only EfficientNet-B4 retains a 95% confidence interval entirely above 0.5. Lip synchronization has the lowest family-level point estimate, although intervals overlap. Seven file-level variables separate the classes (out-of-fold AUC 0.895), yet normalization on a 94-video subset leaves mean detector AUC essentially unchanged (ΔAUC = −0.0008; 95% CI [−0.054, 0.042]). Effort reaches 0.695 on the fixed subset but fails the control and is reported separately. Overall, reproducible public checkpoints transfer poorly to this fixed Arabic-media evaluation domain.

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) benchmarks are not neutral tools of evaluation but socio-technical artefacts that shape competition, power, and research priorities within AI. Benchmarks standardise the assessment of systems and facilitate the creation of leaderboards that reward state-of-the-art performance with prestige, citations, trust, and institutional influence. As the costs of developing competitive AI systems rise, these rewards increasingly concentrate among powerful, industry-funded labs. This paper situates these concerns within Iris Marion Young's theories of oppression and structural injustice. It argues that current benchmarking practices may perpetuate systematic harms affecting various actors in AI research, aligning with four of Young’s "faces of oppression". Benchmarking culture is further framed as a source of structural injustice, as these harms emerge from normalised, individually defensible practices and network effects, even without explicit wrongdoing. By reinforcing existing power structures and narrowing possible research trajectories, benchmarking may in fact prevent the field from advancing in epistemically robust and socially beneficial ways.
evidence_items.title: The Benchmark Trap: Structures of Power and Injustice in AI Evaluations

evidence_items.summary: This research examines how city images of Istanbul’s Historic Peninsula are evolving with artificial intelligence and expanding user-generated content. City image refers to a mental representation of urban structure, and imageability to the ease of forming it. Using Lynch’s five-element framework (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks), the study compares a classical verbal cognitive map based on 32 interviews with built-environment academics (noting possible sample bias) with ChatGPT’s reading of 210 citizen reviews from TripAdvisor and Ekşi Sözlük. A structured, multi-step prompting workflow, guided and checked by humans at each stage, prompts the model (not trained on the corpus) to extract, categorize, and summarize key locations and experiences in these informal narratives. While the model recognizes familiar Lynch elements, it also redistributes their prominence: iconic buildings become less dominant, while comfort, crowding, safety, and spatial atmosphere become more central. The findings suggest that large language models can function as urban observers capable of summarizing collective city images at scale. The method offers a reproducible way to connect interview-based cognitive mapping with platform narratives. It highlights the need for critical, human-led interpretation when applying language models to urban design.

evidence_items.summary: Bile duct hyperplasia in rodents, caused by chemical cytotoxicity, bile flow interference, or aging, is traditionally assessed through time-consuming microscopic examination by pathologists. We developed a deep learning-based, artificial intelligence (AI) model for quick and accurate assessment of bile duct hyperplasia in mice. The study utilized 127 hematoxylin and eosin-stained, mouse liver whole-slide images (WSIs) digitized using Aperio scanners. A segmentation algorithm with a U-Net architecture and an EfficientNet backbone was trained on 1165 areas from 35 WSIs to identify and quantify bile ducts, measure their area percentage using a supervised method, and categorize them into grades 0 to 4 using an unsupervised method. The model was validated on 24 WSIs and tested on 68 WSIs, all independently scored by 3 veterinary pathologists using consensus criteria. The segmentation model achieved Dice scores of 91.75% in training and 85.88% in validation. Testing revealed high sensitivity (95%), specificity (97%), and Dice score (95.45%), indicating robust model accuracy. Model-predicted grades showed strong correlation ( r 2 s = 0.86) with pathologists’ consensus scores. This AI-driven approach has the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of bile duct hyperplasia assessments in rodent studies, paving the way for more standardized, objective, and high-throughput histological evaluations in preclinical research.
evidence_items.title: Comparative evaluation of artificial intelligence-based and pathologist scoring of murine bile duct hyperplasia

evidence_items.summary: This study investigates the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications on buyer–supplier relationship quality in Nigeria's mobile manufacturing sector, with specific reference to TECNO Mobile Nigeria. Drawing on the Commitment-Trust Theory of Relationship Marketing (Morgan & Hunt, 1994), the study operationalises AI through three proxies: Predictive Analytics (PA), Automation of Processes (AP), and AI Risk Management (AIR). A survey research design was adopted, and structured questionnaires were administered to 250 employees and supply chain partners purposively selected from TECNO Mobile's procurement, logistics, IT, and supplier management functions. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (frequencies, means, standard deviations) and one-sample t-tests benchmarked against the scale's neutral midpoint (μ₀ = 3.00). All three null hypotheses were rejected at p < 0.001. Predictive Analytics recorded an aggregate mean of 3.88 (SD = 0.34; t(249) = 40.53), Automation of Processes 3.91 (SD = 0.36; t(249) = 40.05), and AI Risk Management 3.92 (SD = 0.36; t(249) = 40.47), all significantly above the neutral midpoint. Findings confirm that respondents perceive each AI dimension as positively and meaningfully contributing to trust, efficiency, transparency, and long-term relational stability with suppliers. The study contributes empirical evidence from an under-studied domain in the AI-supply chain literature, Nigeria's mobile manufacturing sector, and offers practical guidance for practitioners and policymakers pursuing AI-enabled supply chain transformation in emerging economies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Buyer–Supplier Relationships in Procurement

evidence_items.summary: Introduction: artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how diseases are diagnosed, treated and monitored, integrating machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing into the analysis of large volumes of clinical data. Objective: to comprehensively analyze the impact of artificial intelligence on medicine, examining its main diagnostic, therapeutic and clinical-management applications, as well as the challenges, limitations and ethical considerations that condition its safe, equitable and patient-centered integration. Development: AI has matured most in medical imaging, oncology and precision medicine, complementing rather than replacing clinical judgment; randomized evidence in cardiology shows improved workflow efficiency and reduced adverse events, including all-cause mortality. Implementation nonetheless faces technical, organizational and social barriers—data quality and interoperability, lack of explainability, algorithmic bias, and gaps in clinician training—alongside ethical and regulatory challenges regarding privacy, accountability and informed consent. Conclusions: AI offers considerable potential to reduce costs, increase diagnostic accuracy, personalize care and expand access to quality services, provided its deployment overcomes technical, ethical and regulatory barriers through proactive, adaptive and patient-centered governance.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) holds considerable promise for improving cardiovascular care, but prior to widespread adoption AI-powered tools require evaluation in randomised trials. We systematically reviewed the current evidence from randomised trials of AI tools in cardiovascular medicine. Methods We conducted a systematic review of randomised trials comparing AI tools vs. standard care in cardiovascular medicine. PubMed, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Scopus, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform were searched from January 1, 2018, to April 10, 2026. Screening and full-text review were performed by three independent reviewers and risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2 criteria. Results Of 11,151 identified records, 8,599 remained after removal of duplicates. Following screening and full-text review, 25 trials met the eligibility criteria. These trials evaluated AI tools in acute cardiovascular care (n = 3), cardiac imaging (n = 6), decision support for medical therapy (n = 6), electrophysiology (n = 8), and interventional cardiology (n = 2). Nine trials were single-centre, and two were international. Seventeen trials (68%) reported positive results, defined by non-inferiority or superiority of the AI-based strategy. Overall risk of bias was rated as high or with some concerns in 84% of the included trials, and only 36% explicitly reported following the CONSORT-/SPIRIT-AI reporting guidelines. Discussion Evidence from randomised trials evaluating AI tools in cardiovascular medicine is limited and most trials have a high risk of bias. Wider implementation of AI tools into practice requires robust, international, multi-centre randomised trials that evaluate patient-relevant outcomes, ensure external validity, and adhere to reporting guidelines. Trial registration number: PROSPERO CRD420251019264

evidence_items.summary: Despite scientific argumentation being a fundamental competency of the PISA assessment framework, prospective biology teachers often demonstrate insufficient development in evidence-based reasoning and rebuttal construction skills. Considering the limitations of large-scale implementation of individualized approaches in higher education, this study evaluates the effectiveness of Generative Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT-4) configured as a “Socratic tutor” in developing argumentation skills among future educators. An 8-week quasi-experimental study involving 124 students from a pedagogical university employed traditional peer discussion methods in the control group ( n = 62), while the experimental group ( n = 62) utilized an AI agent that induced cognitive dissonance regarding socio-scientific issues. Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) of data obtained through Toulmin's Argument Pattern (TAP) and PISA rubrics confirmed that the experimental group achieved statistically significantly higher overall argumentation quality compared to the control group (F (1,121) = 14.23, p &lt; .001, η 2 = .105). Particularly, participants who received AI-assisted instruction showed marked improvement in forming rebuttals and evaluating counterevidence, which are considered among the most cognitively demanding components within the PISA scientific literacy framework (OECD). These findings suggest that a Generative AI-mediated Socratic instructional package can be an effective and scalable approach for developing epistemic cognition, and they propose a pedagogical model for integrating structured AI-based tutoring into teacher preparation systems aligned with international assessment standards.

evidence_items.summary: Groundwater plays a critical role in meeting drinking and agricultural water demands in India. This review focuses on regional variations in groundwater quality, contamination sources, and remediation strategies. The evaluation encompasses pH, electrical conductivity, total dissolved solids, hardness, major ions, and contaminants including fluoride, arsenic, nitrate, and heavy metals. Results reveal significant regional variations, with contamination driven by intensive agriculture, industrial activities, mining, urbanization, and geological factors. Water Quality Index assessments indicate that while many groundwater sources meet drinking standards, numerous sites exceed permissible limits, requiring treatment. Contamination stems from both natural processes (mineral dissolution and rock–water interactions) and anthropogenic activities (fertilizer application, industrial effluents, domestic sewage, and mining operations). Health risk assessments demonstrate elevated noncarcinogenic risks in fluoride- and nitrate-affected areas, causing fluorosis, arsenicosis, methemoglobinemia, and other waterborne diseases. Various remediation approaches suitable for Indian conditions have been investigated, including membrane-based systems, electrochemical methods, adsorption techniques, and nature-based solutions. This review provides an integrated understanding of India’s regional groundwater quality challenges and emphasizes the necessity for targeted interventions, enhanced monitoring, and sustainable management strategies to protect groundwater resources. The review further provides an integrated regional comparison framework linking contamination sources, hydrogeochemical processes, health risks, and remediation strategies for groundwater management in India.
evidence_items.title: Groundwater Contamination in India: Regional Variations, Hydrogeochemical Controls, Health Risks, and Integrated Management Strategies

evidence_items.summary: Measuring welfare in the informal sector can be biased when it relies on fluctuating nominal income rather than actual household expenditure. This study applies the Capability Approach to examine how resources shape the economic functioning of informal worker households in Gunungkidul, Indonesia, using real household consumption expenditure as a proxy for functioning. The study contributes by shifting the unit of analysis to households and introducing the District Minimum Wage (UMK) as a conceptual benchmark. Using March 2025 National Socioeconomic Survey (Susenas) data covering 464 informal worker households, the study applies binary logistic regression. The model shows good discriminatory capacity, with an AUC of 0.788 and a Nagelkerke R-squared of 0.321. Male-headed households have substantially higher odds of achieving expenditure above the UMK. Financial inclusion shows contrasting effects: account ownership is negatively associated with the outcome, while credit, digital money, and combined financial services are positively associated, with combined services showing the largest odds ratio. Business-oriented internet use has a stronger positive association than general internet access. Higher education and longer working hours are positively associated with the probability of expenditure above the UMK, whereas age has a negative association. The findings highlight the importance of human capital, productive financial inclusion, business-oriented digitalization, and demographic characteristics in expanding the economic capabilities of informal worker households.
evidence_items.title: Determinants of Economic Functioning among Informal Worker Households Using the District Minimum Wage as a Benchmark: Empirical Evidence from Gunungkidul

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Ultrasonic communication through steel has emerged as a technically challenging but operationally transformative capability for subsea inspection and monitoring. This paper focuses on an ultrasonic system for transmitting high-rate data from a smart pig through steel barriers in a subsea environment, examining phased-array beamforming, array geometry, mounting strategies, signal design, and model- led performance evaluation. The work presented here reflects the current stage of the research, which remains simulation-driven but is now transitioning toward hardware prototyping and experimental validation. The paper presents a detailed analysis of 1D and 2D phased-array behaviour, including the influence of element spacing, aperture size, curvature, and mounting configuration on beam focus, energy delivery, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Analytical and numerical simulations, along with a fully parametric 3D model for finite element analysis (FEA), are used to refine the design and quantify the expected performance. The results demonstrate that phased-array beamforming can significantly improve energy delivery through steel, enabling high-bandwidth ultrasonic communication through metal barriers. The paper also examines the use of high-performance Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) encoding for ultrasonic communication, the implementation of row-column addressing for large arrays, and the integration of high-voltage drivers and low- noise receiver electronics. The paper underscores research maturity, technical depth, and the pragmatic considerations essential for transitioning from modelling to prototype development and concludes with a roadmap for this next research phase.
evidence_items.title: Directional Data: Ultrasonic Beamforming to Unlock Pipeline Inspection Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Cyclic Steam Stimulation (CSS) is widely applied in heavy oil reservoirs to reduce oil viscosity and restore production through repeated steam injection, soak, and production cycles. In multilayer reservoirs, however, steam can preferentially enter shallow, depleted, watered-out, or higher-permeability intervals, resulting in poor steam conformance, excessive water production, and limited stimulation of deeper target zones. This paper presents a three-well field application where high-temperature thermal tubular patch technology was deployed to isolate shallow perforated intervals and redirect steam into deeper productive layers. The system comprises blank tubular sections with hydraulically expanded metal-to-metal sealing elements at both ends, providing a robust internal barrier capable of withstanding repeated high-temperature steam cycles. The workflow included production-history review, casing diagnostics, patch placement design, hydraulic expansion, post-installation verification, and production surveillance after CSS restart. The three pilot wells achieved peak oil-rate improvements of approximately 179%, 292%, and 242% compared with pre-intervention baselines, together with water-cut reductions from 97% to 88%, 98% to 90%, and 96% to 68%, respectively. The results confirm improved steam placement, successful shallow-zone isolation, and material production uplift. The intervention also demonstrated strong indicative economics, with a combined incremental oil rate of 482 BOPD and short payback sensitivity under reasonable netback assumptions. The work establishes a scalable intervention model for CSS well rejuvenation by applying a metal-to-metal thermal tubular patch to redirect steam into deeper target intervals.
evidence_items.title: Rejuvenating Steam Inflow Performance in Cyclic Steam Stimulation Wells Using Innovative Thermal Tubular Patch Technology: A New Benchmark for Heavy Oil Wells

evidence_items.summary: Objectives: Patients and clinicians increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) about Kampo, Japan's traditional medicine. Yet evaluations of LLMs have measured accuracy on examination questions, which ask what a model knows; a consultation asks whether it can apply that knowledge to the patient at hand. No benchmark had measured that. Materials and Methods: KampoBench comprises 74 consultation scenarios and 310 conversation-specific rubric criteria, following the design of HealthBench. Scenarios, criteria and reference answers were drafted by an LLM and revised by board-certified Kampo physicians. Ten current models from three vendors were evaluated. Because LLM graders are known to favor their own family, each response was graded by a model from each vendor. Results: The best model reached 74.8-86.3% across graders, the physician-revised reference answers 87.9-92.4%. Rankings were stable across graders (Spearman's rho 0.952-0.976), and the family-favoring deviation was 0.4 to 0.6 percentage points, below the bootstrap standard deviation of one measurement; grader leniency varied by 14.3 points. Models were most reliable on criteria about advising that care be sought (83.6%) and least reliable on those requiring a known crude-drug risk to be tied to the case (17.5%), though 79.2% of those responses named the drug. Discussion: The shortfall lay in applying knowledge to the case rather than in holding it - a distinction examination-format evaluations cannot make. Conclusion: Evaluation in traditional medicine should measure the judgments a consultation requires, not recall alone. Quoted alongside the grader that produced it, a KampoBench score is a usable measure of those judgments.
evidence_items.title: From examinations to consultations: a physician-reviewed Japanese benchmark for large language models in traditional Kampo medicine

evidence_items.summary: Conventional forecasting methods are trained end-to-end on unimodal time series, which limits their ability to exploit textual information and undermines their generalization in data-scarce scenarios. Recently, large language models (LLMs) and time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated powerful capabilities in complex textual reasoning and zero-shot temporal modeling, respectively. Integrating these strengths to construct a multimodal time series foundation model that jointly leverages temporal and textual information for zero-shot future inference has emerged as a promising research direction. However, the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality multimodal datasets remains a fundamental obstacle. To address this challenge, we propose ChronoSteer, a decoupled agentic framework that learns cross-modal alignment from synthetic paired supervision. Specifically, a pretrained LLM first converts textual events into revision instructions that steer the initial unimodal prediction produced by a frozen TSFM. These revision instructions form an intermediate instruction space that bridges the semantic gap between text and time series while fully leveraging pretrained knowledge. Technically, the instructions are discretized into a compact codebook of instruction anchors, effectively mitigating semantic divergence while reducing the cost of dataset construction. Finally, we adopt a two-stage training strategy to recover the fine-grained magnitude information lost during discretization. Furthermore, we release a leakage-controlled multimodal benchmark constructed with temporal separation and textual context available before the prediction window. When paired with an LLM and trained on synthetic cross-modal alignment data, ChronoSteer achieves a 25.8% improvement in zero-shot prediction accuracy over its unimodal backbone, and outperforms prior state-of-the-art unimodal and multimodal methods by 17.8% and 22.5%.
evidence_items.title: ChronoSteer: Bridging Large Language Model and Time Series Foundation Model via Synthetic Cross-Modal Alignment Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background This study aimed to develop and externally validate an instruction-tuned multimodal large language model (MLLM) for early warning and early diagnosis of dry eye disease (DED) using routinely obtainable clinical data. Methods A total of 874 participants were enrolled, including an internal development cohort (n = 743) from Peking University Third Hospital (October 2024 to August 2025) and an independent external validation cohort (n = 131) from three additional centers. Participants included both DED and non-DED individuals, diagnosed according to the Chinese Expert Consensus (2020) and TFOS DEWS II criteria. We developed DED-MLLM on the basis of Qwen2-VL and constructed a domain-specific instruction-tuning dataset integrating Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI), Standard Patient Evaluation of Eye Dryness (SPEED), self-reported questionnaires, ophthalmic imaging, and clinical examination data. Model performance was evaluated for risk stratification and diagnosis under both diagnostic frameworks, with ablation analyses used to examine the relative contributions of visual and structured clinical modalities. Results Based on the international diagnostic criteria for DED, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.8232 for early warning (specificity: 0.6873, sensitivity: 0.9558) and an accuracy of 0.9203 for diagnosis (specificity: 0.8776, sensitivity: 0.9720). According to the Chinese diagnostic criteria for DED, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.9584 for early warning (specificity: 0.9112, sensitivity: 0.9927) and an accuracy of 0.9327 for diagnosis (specificity: 0.8742, sensitivity: 0.9851). External validation showed AUCs of 0.910 and 0.957 for early warning and 0.960 and 0.893 for diagnosis. Ablation analyses indicated that structured clinical information contributed most strongly to diagnostic performance, whereas image-based information provided complementary, interpretable ocular-surface evidence.
evidence_items.title: Development of a Multimodal Large Language Model for Early Warning and Diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease

evidence_items.summary: Human personality inventories are increasingly used to characterize large language models (LLMs), compare systems, and inform downstream governance claims. Yet, these inventories were developed and validated for humans, and it remains unclear whether they are valid for non-human systems. We present a systematic psychometric evaluation of Big Five personality measurement in LLMs. We ask three research questions: Do Big Five inventories a) appropriately describe LLMs, b) capture meaningful differences between models, and c) reflect internal factors consistent with human personality? We assess the content validity of five candidate Big Five inventories and administer the best-performing inventory to N = 264 LLMs spanning 50 model families. Our findings are threefold. First, Big Five items adapted for LLMs achieve acceptable content validity, whereas the original human-developed items do not. Second, Big Five inventories fail to capture meaningful differences across LLMs: between-model variance accounts for only 7% - 17% of the total score variance. Third, LLMs responses do not reproduce the canonical Big Five five-factor structure of human personality, with four of the five personality facets collapsing into one (r >= .90). Moreover, comparisons between base and instruction-tuned variants suggest that alignment training shifts Big Five scores toward socially desirable profiles. These findings demonstrate that Big Five inventories do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs. Thus, using human personality frameworks to characterize, benchmark, compare, or govern LLMs risks producing misleading conclusions. We highlight the need for evaluation frameworks that are specifically designed and validated for LLMs, rather than transferring human psychological constructs without first establishing their validity.
evidence_items.title: Personality Without Persons? A Psychometric Critique of Big Five Testing in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Existing LLM safety benchmarks focus primarily on English and Western contexts, often overlooking the linguistic diversity and culturally grounded safety risks present in other languages. We introduce SurakshaEval, a novel safety benchmark composed of human-written prompts spanning real-world scenarios, explicitly designed for ten major Indian languages - Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Telugu, along with English. We benchmark state-of-the-art LLMs on SurakshaEval, establishing safety baselines and identifying recurring failure modes, including over-refusal and insufficient contextual awareness in regionally sensitive settings, particularly in native scripts. These findings underscore the need for region-specific data and structured evaluations to build safe, ethical, and culturally aligned AI systems. Warning: This paper contains potentially offensive or unsafe content.
evidence_items.title: SurakshaEval: An Indic Safety Benchmark for Multilingual LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is currently undergoing exponential development that operates beyond traditional CPU transistor benchmarks like Moore's Law, propelled instead by domain-specific architectural scaling (Huang's Law) and massive cluster aggregation. This research investigates the divergence and convergence between Large Language Model (LLM) projections and human perceptions regarding a post-singularity future. Utilizing a hybrid phenomenological qualitative and quantitative methodology, we interviewed five major LLMs—Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet, OpenAI GPT-4o, Google Gemini 2.0 Flash, Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4), and xAI Grok 3—alongside a purposive sample of ten human participants. We introduced a persona-steering protocol to evaluate model output sensitivity when default corporate Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) politeness framing is stripped away, disclosing a pronounced shift towards more aggressive, urgent, and fatalistic narrative clusters. Findings show that while independent qualitative responses from humans and LLMs exhibited limited vocabulary overlap, participants displayed high agreement when subsequently evaluated against collated LLM future scenarios. This indicates a considerable "control risk", pointing to possible vulnerabilities concerning disinformation, liability, and the decline of human cognitive sovereignty. By documenting attitudes during the 2024–2025 acceleration period, this investigation identifies structural friction between technical AI capability expansion and public risk perception, offering an empirical foundation for future studies on cognitive sovereignty and human-AI alignment.
evidence_items.title: Human Perceptions Compared to Large Language Models on the Future of Artificial Intelligence: A Phenomenological Comparative Study

evidence_items.summary: Electronic Product Code Information Services (EPCIS) standardizes inter-organizational supply-chain visibility events, yet structurally conformant histories can contain contradictory lifecycle claims that undermine information integrity. We present EPCIS-MutBench, a controlled benchmark and layered validator for evaluating security-relevant semantic and lifecycle integrity in EPCIS 2.0.1 histories. Mutations are treated as integrity violations independently of accidental or adversarial origin; the benchmark evaluates detection and localization rather than attacker attribution. The evaluation uses 2000 deterministic clean histories and 20,000 primary mutants, including 16,000 single-fault and 4000 compound cases, with validator-independent typed ground truth. Across all primary mutants, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Schema plus compatibility-projected GS1 Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) detected 18.27%, whereas the full event-local and role-aware lifecycle validator detected 95.29%. Among 13,429 single-fault mutants that passed both structural baselines, the full validator achieved 92.98% recall, with end-to-end intended-rule, event, and field/edge localization of 92.90%, 92.19%, and 92.14%, respectively. No false positives occurred on the 2000 generated-clean controls; however, in a separate sensitivity analysis that provisionally treated all 37 parseable external-source fixtures as clean, 19 were marked invalid. A separate attestation layer used cryptographic hashes, Merkle commitments, a digital signature, and public-testnet receipts to make post-freeze evidence modification detectable. The results demonstrate controlled, reproducible evaluation of EPCIS information-integrity assurance beyond structural conformance.
evidence_items.title: EPCIS-MutBench: A Controlled Benchmark for Security-Relevant Semantic and Lifecycle Integrity Validation in EPCIS 2.0.1 Supply-Chain Histories

evidence_items.summary: Modern AI systems depend on annotated data, but annotation is rarely treated as the act of measurement that it is. Instead, annotation quality is commonly reduced to agreement: if multiple annotators assign the same annotation to a data instance, the annotations are taken to be high-quality. Yet agreement does not establish whether annotations validly capture the underlying concept they are meant to represent. In this paper, we argue that data annotation should be understood as a measurement problem. Like other forms of measurement, annotation requires defining a concept, operationalizing it through an instrument, applying that instrument, and evaluating the reliability and validity of the resulting measurements. Drawing on a literature review of annotation quality research (N=132) and semi-structured interviews with annotation team members (N=10), we develop a framework for diagnosing and correcting annotation issues. First, we map key decision points across annotation processes - including task design, annotator management, quality assessment, quality improvement, and adjudication - that shape annotation outcomes. Second, we identify five distinct sources of annotation issues: error, ambiguity, impossibility, subjectivity, and annotator identity. Annotation problems that appear similar at the level of outcomes often require different process-level interventions based on their sources. Finally, we translate measurement theory into practical guidance for annotation teams, showing how assessments of reliability and validity can move beyond agreement alone. By reframing annotation as measurement, we offer a conceptual foundation for improving the quality of annotated data used in AI research and practice.
evidence_items.title: Data Annotation as Measurement

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are making it easier for the public to interact with government, such as by helping them apply for benefits, understand complex policies, and make their opinions heard. Although improving service accessibility is beneficial, any resulting surges in demand could strain unprepared government services. We term such surges "agentic flooding" of government services (''flooding'') and provide three contributions. First, based on a collected dataset of 84 potential cases of flooding across 11 jurisdictions, we posit that flooding is likely occurring widely today, mostly through large language models (LLMs) generating text cheaply. Second, we evaluate what services are most exposed to flooding. We develop a risk matrix to analyze a service's exposure, and suggest that near-term risk is highest for financially attractive, but complex services. Finally, we map possible government responses to flooding. Precedent suggests these responses will likely be sufficient to stop most cases of flooding, but the fastest to deploy – friction-inducing measures like fees – often trade off equitable access to public services. Accordingly, we close by recommending near-term actions that may allow governments to mitigate flooding without invoking this trade-off.
evidence_items.title: Characterizing Agentic Flooding of Government Services

evidence_items.summary: This study develops a safety-aware supervisory framework for industrial fed-batch bioreactors by integrating an adaptive digital twin, fuzzy multi-objective optimization, Agentic LLM reasoning, and an independent Safety Governor within a closed-loop architecture. The digital twin continuously reconstructs process states and updates sensitive parameters, while α-cut fuzzy intervals preserve biological and operational uncertainty throughout prediction and optimization. The Agentic LLM coordinates prediction, optimization, process knowledge, and candidate evaluation, and supports context-dependent reevaluation and replanning as operating conditions evolve. The framework was evaluated using data from 12 industrial 72 h fed-batch runs, together with 600 uncertainty-aware simulated trajectories. Across three fully independent validation batches, the digital twin achieved an average NRMSE of 4.7%, MAPE of 4.4%, and R2 of 0.985. Closed-loop operation achieved a volumetric productivity of 0.347 g/L·h while maintaining a positive minimum dissolved-oxygen margin of 5 percentage points and zero hard-constraint violations. Across nominal and stressed scenarios, the Safety Governor preserved feasible operation with no residual hard-constraint violations, while the Agentic LLM successfully activated reevaluation and replanning following changes in process conditions. The ablation results further showed that the complete architecture provided the strongest overall balance among productivity, biological risk, robustness, and disturbance recovery. These findings demonstrate the value of combining adaptive process representation, uncertainty-aware optimization, agentic supervisory reasoning, and independent safety validation for reliable intelligent bioprocess operation.
evidence_items.title: A Safety-Aware Agentic LLM–Digital Twin Framework for Fuzzy Multi-Objective Control of Industrial Fed-Batch Bioreactors

evidence_items.summary: Hallucinated information can propagate through multi-stage LLM systems and become part of the context for subsequent reasoning. Existing studies of post-hallucination reasoning (PHR) mainly characterize changes in final outcomes and aggregate reasoning dynamics, leaving how models resolve hallucinated premises at the response level insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce PHRBench, a controlled benchmark for behaviorally structured PHR across four domains and 18 large language models. PHRBench characterizes each reasoning trajectory independently of final-answer correctness through Hallucination Compliance, Hallucination Avoidance, and Heuristic Correction, and defines an insightful trajectory as successful correction that ultimately reaches the correct answer. Across 4820 controlled instances, we find that successful recovery remains relatively rare and is associated with more frequent belief updates along the reasoning trajectory. We further find that properties of the hallucinated prompt contain substantial predictive signal for successful recovery, with a lightweight predictor achieving an AUROC of 0.847. These findings provide a behavioral view of post-hallucination reasoning, characterizing how LLMs resolve erroneous context and when successful recovery is likely to occur.
evidence_items.title: PHRBench: A Behavioral Evaluation of Post-Hallucination Reasoning in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Automated failure attribution uses LLMs to identify where and why agentic systems fail. As agents become more capable, their failures become subtler, making automated attribution increasingly important. We introduce Who&When Pro, a large-scale benchmark for automated failure attribution in agentic systems. Using a strictly controlled pipeline that injects a failure only after exactly replaying a successful prefix, we construct 12,326 failed trajectories with golden labels across 3 modalities and 26 benchmarks covering various scenarios. Beyond benchmarking, we conduct extensive experiments and analyses, revealing systematic patterns in how models attribute failures across modalities, protocols, and model families, and providing empirical guidance for future automated failure attribution systems.
evidence_items.title: Who&When Pro: Can LLMs Really Attribute Failures in AI Agents?

evidence_items.summary: Recent Audio Multimodal Large Language Models (Audio MLLMs) demonstrate impressive performance on speech benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether these models genuinely process acoustic signals or rely on text-based semantic inference. To systematically study this question, we introduce DEAF (Diagnostic Evaluation of Acoustic Faithfulness), a benchmark of over 2,700 conflict stimuli spanning three acoustic dimensions: emotional prosody, background sounds, and speaker identity. Then, we design a controlled multi-level evaluation framework that progressively increases textual influence, ranging from semantic conflicts in the content to misleading prompts and their combination, allowing us to disentangle content-driven bias from prompt-induced sycophancy. We further introduce diagnostic metrics to quantify model reliance on textual cues over acoustic signals. Our evaluation of seven Audio MLLMs reveals a consistent pattern of text dominance: models are sensitive to acoustic variations, yet predictions are predominantly driven by textual inputs, revealing a gap between high performance on standard speech benchmarks and genuine acoustic understanding.
evidence_items.title: DEAF: A Benchmark for Diagnostic Evaluation of Acoustic Faithfulness in Audio Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Current test-time scaling (TTS) techniques enhance large language model (LLM) performance by allocating additional computation at inference time, yet they remain insufficient for agentic settings, where actions directly interact with external environments and their effects can be irreversible and costly. We propose ARTIS, Agentic Risk-Aware Test-Time Scaling via Iterative Simulation, a framework that decouples exploration from commitment by enabling test-time exploration through simulated interactions prior to real-world execution. This design allows extending inference-time computation to improve action-level reliability and robustness without incurring environmental risk. We further show that naive LLM-based simulators struggle to capture rare but high-impact failure modes, substantially limiting their effectiveness for agentic decision making. To address this limitation, we introduce a risk-aware tool simulator that emphasizes fidelity on failure-inducing actions via targeted data generation and rebalanced training. Experiments on multi-turn and multi-step agentic benchmarks demonstrate that iterative simulation substantially improves agent reliability, and that risk-aware simulation is essential for consistently realizing these gains across models and tasks.
evidence_items.title: ARTIS: Agentic Risk-Aware Test-Time Scaling via Iterative Simulation

evidence_items.summary: Existing LLM-based agent approaches for long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single-session execution lengthens, the agent's reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long-horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. These findings suggest that their benefits may not persist across versions, which motivates a workflow-level approach in which agents build on one another's work across sessions. We model these alternating agent sessions as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP) and establish sufficient conditions for alternation to exceed single-agent reference limits, derive an explicit experiment-budget bound, and characterize when session caps preserve this advantage. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which alternates two agents on a shared workspace, limits each session to at most k experiments and resets the context between sessions, without additional task-specific harness or prior knowledge supplements. Across 75 Kaggle tasks in MLE-bench, HMA reaches a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 8.0 points with a quarter of its time budget. Moreover, among six configurations spanning five heterogeneous agent pairs, HMA improves any-medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.4 points on average, demonstrating cross-pair generality. A supplementary case on kernel optimization reaches 878 cycles, within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader, demonstrating applicability beyond MLE.
evidence_items.title: Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits

evidence_items.summary: The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based methods in robotic manipulation. Over short horizons, it demands precise, contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts. Over long horizons, it requires recovery and coordination across extended action sequences. Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have enabled research advances by providing guidance on how to assemble. But how much of the strategy must be specified? The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that RL at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win. AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward and task diversity admitted by this task-agnostic reward can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble. In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1, reaching 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning. The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, with task success rewarded only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete. The learned policies discover dexterous and planning-like behaviors: choosing grasps for later assembly, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and preparing one part, assembling another, then returning to finish the first without an explicit planner. For videos, see our website: https://alpha-nist.github.io/
evidence_items.title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards

evidence_items.summary: Medical image segmentation is undergoing a paradigm shift from conventional visual pattern matching to cognitive reasoning analysis. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown promise in integrating linguistic and visual knowledge, significant gaps remain: existing general MLLMs possess broad common sense but lack the specialized visual reasoning required for complex lesions, whereas traditional segmentation models excel at pixel-level segmentation but lack logical interpretability. In this paper, we introduce ComLesion-14K, the first diverse Chain-of-Thought (CoT) benchmark for reasoning-driven complex lesion segmentation. To accomplish this task, we propose CORE-Seg, an end-to-end framework integrating reasoning with segmentation through a Semantic-Guided Prompt Adapter. We design a progressive training strategy from SFT to GRPO, equipped with an adaptive dual-granularity reward mechanism to mitigate reward sparsity. evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Automated visual inspection of pharmaceutical tablets is increasingly important for detecting manufacturing defects and maintaining consistent product quality. Progress in artificial intelligence-based defect classification is, however, constrained by the scarcity of publicly accessible image datasets covering defective tablets under diverse visual conditions. This study introduces the PharmaVision (PV) dataset, a public visual dataset and benchmark for classifying normal and defective compressed tablets. Methods: The PV dataset contains 640 smartphone-acquired images spanning varied tablet products, backgrounds, and lighting, with fixed tablet-level splits (190/190 training, 30/30 validation, and 100/100 test images for the normal and defective classes, respectively). Twelve representative architectures spanning classical convolutional networks, mobile networks, and vision transformers were benchmarked under an identical protocol using accuracy, precision, recall, and harmonic mean of precision and recall (F1-score), with 95% confidence intervals and paired statistical tests. Cross-dataset generalization was assessed on the independent pillQC dataset without fine-tuning, and efficiency was profiled using parameters, Giga floating-point operations (GFLOPs), latency, and throughput. Results: EfficientNetV2-S achieved the highest F1-score on the PV test set (88.56%), although paired statistical tests did not distinguish it from Xception (87.08%) or Swin-B (85.71%). On pillQC, GoogLeNet and EfficientNetV2-S showed the strongest cross-dataset performance, whereas both vision transformers declined relative to their in-domain results. AlexNet gave the highest theoretical throughput (602.41 frames per second (FPS), median latency 1.66 ms), whereas ShuffleNetV2 and MobileNetV3-small offered the smallest parameter counts.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Quality Control of Pharmaceutical Tablets: A Visual Dataset and Benchmark for Automated Defect Detection
