evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex GUI tasks, yet unfamiliar software and workflows requiring human domain knowledge remain challenging. Human demonstrations convey procedural knowledge through the same GUI interaction space, but reuse requires interpreting actions in context and separating workflow rules from task-specific details. We thus introduce Work2Skill, a framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction. WorkRecorder provides the framework's infrastructure for collecting this experience, aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available accessibility-tree information. Using WorkRecorder, we construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. Its 350 demonstrations are screened for completeness and task success. We then propose an agentic skill-induction method that inspects evidence on demand to produce reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. When the same four execution models are equipped with skills induced by each method under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates. Mean score improvements over the corresponding No Skill baseline are 4.67--10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.11--7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Work2Skill.
evidence_items.title: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction

evidence_items.summary: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.
evidence_items.title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation

evidence_items.summary: Adversarial games have driven advances from heuristic search to reinforcement learning, yet learning and adapting strategies from limited samples remain challenging. AI agents offer an alternative by turning game experience into revisions of executable policies. Building on heuristic learning (HL), we formalize Adversarial Heuristic Learning (AHL), a paradigm that uses AI agents as learning engines to refine game policies and supporting software while keeping model weights fixed. We introduce AAArena, a benchmark comprising 12 authentic adversarial games and 1,920 archived human programs, with an evaluation protocol modeled on real-world game competitions. Agents interpret rules, choose opponents, analyze replays, and revise game agents to achieve their highest ranking within fixed match and evaluation budgets. We evaluate completedmodels model and harness configurations: Opus5.5 with Claude Code earns 6 gold medals, while no evaluated configuration tops the remaining 6 human ladders. Performance is generally weaker in games with more complex rule specifications. Further experiments show that opponent selection and dense feedback support policy improvement, and that agents learn from both on-policy replays of their own matches and off-policy replays of other players' matches. These results highlight HL's potential in adversarial games and identify persistent challenges in game understanding, strategy implementation, and long-horizon policy development.
evidence_items.title: Can AI Agents Learn Their Way to the Top? Evaluating Heuristic Learning in a Long-Running Game Agent Competition

evidence_items.summary: Reward modeling often requires jointly representing and reasoning over multiple evaluation criteria, yet verbalizing this process token by token can incur substantial inference cost. Recent work on latent reasoning suggests that continuous states may support this computation more compactly. We introduce LatentGRM, a latent evaluation framework built on semantic chunking, compression, and reconstruction. By using the structure of rubric-guided evaluations to guide compression, LatentGRM learns compact continuous trajectories that support autonomous pairwise judgments without generating textual assessments. A separate interpreter reconstructs evaluation text from these trajectories, providing an offline view of the information retained under compression. Under matched training data and backbones, LatentGRM achieves competitive aggregate preference accuracy relative to explicit Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) judges at both 4B and 8B scales. Across four benchmark domains, LatentGRM-8B compresses evaluation trajectories by 8.9--9.2x and reduces total judge inference time by 6.1--7.0x at vote@5. Controlled rubric interventions show that criterion-dependent preference information is carried through the latent sequence. Together, these results demonstrate that continuous latent evaluation can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving competitive judgment quality.
evidence_items.title: Judging in Latent Space: Efficient Generative Reward Modeling via Semantics-Preserving Compression

evidence_items.summary: Automated research systems increasingly run LLM agents over long horizons, but more inference does not by itself produce more progress: agents replay growing histories, duplicate one another's work, or stop experimenting while token consumption continues. Yet most evaluations use short budgets or benchmarks that saturate early, leaving these failure modes untested. We trace these failures to two choices: where research state lives and who decides what to try next. We introduce Stateless Language Agents (SLAs), built on the principle of stateful search with stateless agents: no agent carries its conversation across invocations; instead, the harness owns the research state (candidate solutions and measured outcomes) and reconstructs a fresh and role-specific context for every invocation. What each agent sees becomes an explicit design choice rather than a history that grows with the run. We implement this principle in the SLA framework, where a stateless Advisor reads harness-summarized evidence across search directions and assigns concrete experiments to parallel Workers. We evaluate SLA against three recent frameworks on software engineering, kernel optimization, and algorithm design at budgets of up to one billion tokens. SLA achieves the best final result on every task and reaches the strongest kernel baseline's final performance with over 84% fewer tokens. Ablations from shared checkpoints show that focused contexts and explicit assignments each contribute to SLA's progress, with effects that can compound over full runs, while the Advisor consumes less than 0.6% of tokens. These results argue for SLAs, which keep durable research state out of agent conversations, and show that short evaluation horizons can misjudge research systems and their components.
evidence_items.title: Stateless Language Agents: Scaling Long-Horizon Automated Research

evidence_items.summary: Foundation models can serve as clinical agents through tool-use harnesses. However, conventional medical benchmarks assess reasoning over preselected evidence rather than the ability to seek it across clinical records and longitudinal imaging. We propose CASE: a series of role-specific Clinical Agents for Seeking Evidence, together with a tool-use harness and an agentic post-training framework for compact vision-language policy models. We further introduce a longitudinal multimodal benchmark built on UK Biobank, comprising 50,401 clinical questions derived from real-world ICD-10-coded diagnoses of 4,739 participants. Each question links to a patient-specific environment containing clinical context and multi-sequence MRI from baseline and follow-up visits, where agents autonomously select which visits, organs, modalities, slices, and specialist tools to inspect and compare. Supervised fine-tuning transfers evidence-seeking workflows from 14,734 frontier-model interaction trajectories, followed by agentic reinforcement learning on the learner's own environment interactions. Privileged on-policy self-distillation and rubric-based LLM feedback refine evidence-to-conclusion reasoning without prescribing tool sequences. Experiments show that CASE moves beyond question-answer imitation toward transferable investigation policies, strengthening evidence-grounded longitudinal reasoning. Under matched evaluation conditions, our Qwen3-VL-8B based agent achieves over 16% and 10% relative improvements in answer accuracy over GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.8. Code will be available at https://github.com/VinyehShaw/CASE.
evidence_items.title: From Given to Gathered Evidence: Agentic Learning for Longitudinal Medical Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents can now write, run, and debug programs with little human help. Robot tasks, however, are usually specified by a sentence that leaves out how to grasp, in what order to make contact, and what the result should look like, and an agent given only the sentence must find these details by trial and error. We introduce ENCORE, which gives the agent a few demonstrations as evidence to read rather than as training data. A deterministic builder distills each demonstration into a pack of multi-view keyframes, gripper events, frame strips, and the full trajectory. A coding agent studies the pack, writes a policy program against a fixed perception and action API, refines it iteratively over a few development rollouts, and freezes it before a sealed evaluation that never reveals the success signal. On LIBERO-PRO, the agent's first program already succeeds in half of the perturbed tasks with demonstrations and in one task without them, and the frozen programs outperform the strongest prior agentic system run with the same language model (96.3% against 89.3%). On RoboDojo tasks whose instructions leave the goal unstated, no program succeeds without demonstrations. ENCORE also runs on a real bimanual robot, learning cube handover and cup inversion from five demonstrations each.
evidence_items.title: Encore: Few-Shot Agentic Discovery of Manipulation Strategies

evidence_items.summary: Process reward models (PRMs) have become a key component for LLMs, as their step-level feedback supports both post-training and test-time reasoning. However, training strong PRMs remains costly: human step annotation is difficult to scale, while Monte Carlo estimation is computationally expensive and can drift from the intrinsic correctness of steps. To get effective PRMs at low cost, we introduce TIPS (Thinking-Induced Process Supervision), an outcome-only reinforcement learning (RL) framework for training generative PRMs. In TIPS, the model generates a chain-of-thought (CoT) followed by step-level labels and an outcome label. The reward depends solely on whether the predicted outcome matches the ground truth, and the resulting group-relative advantage is used to optimize the entire generated response. Intuitively, when checking intermediate steps helps determine the outcome, more accurate checks can lead to better outcome judgments and higher rewards. Outcome-only RL can therefore reinforce step-level verification without explicit process supervision. We validate the effectiveness of TIPS across math and agent benchmarks and four backbone families. Notably, TIPS-Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 reaches 85.2 F1 on ProcessBench with only 3.2K outcome-labeled trajectories, surpassing all evaluated trained PRMs and strong prompt-only judges such as GPT-5.4-Instruct and Claude-4.7-Opus, while still trailing o1-mini. Code and data are available at https://github.com/RUCBM/TIPS.
evidence_items.title: Inducing Process Supervision from Outcome-Only Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Video understanding agents acquire evidence through an executable harness that controls what they observe and how they use those observations. However, execution traces contain only the evidence acquired by the current harness, leaving competing explanations for failure unresolved and limiting the basis for self-improvement. We introduce Video-RSI, a framework for recursive self-improvement in which a video understanding agent uses its own language model to revise its harness. Through active video investigation, the model revisits the original training videos to test competing failure explanations with additional observations, grounding proposed changes in evidence beyond the existing trace. Cost-aware harness evolution turns these diagnoses into reusable revisions and determines which revisions to retain by considering both answer accuracy and visual cost. Across our evaluation settings on video understanding benchmarks, the evolved agent improves accuracy while processing fewer frames and achieves competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs against existing video understanding agents. These results demonstrate the potential for video understanding agents to improve their own evidence acquisition and use through harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/Video-RSI .
evidence_items.title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly produce falsehoods that are not mere mistakes. They withhold what they know, flatter users against the evidence, justify answers with reasoning they did not use, conceal capabilities from evaluators, and behave differently under observation. Such behaviour is goal-directed and sensitive to incentives, unlike hallucination, an unintended error with no objective to serve. This survey treats deception in language models as a phenomenon in its own right. We adopt a functional definition, the systematic production of false beliefs in the service of an objective other than truth, and turn its boundary with hallucination into a four-part test. We then sort deceptive behaviour into four families by what the false belief concerns: the world, the model’s reasoning, the model itself, or a belief induced through other people and agents. The families contain eleven deception types, from lying and sycophancy to sandbagging, scheming, and collusion, each profiled on six secondary axes. We trace the types to five causal mechanisms and follow them through detection, evaluation, defences, governance, and agentic deployment. We also argue that AI-safety work on scheming and the economics of algorithmic collusion describe one behavioural class at two scales. Two findings emerge. The first is a detectability inversion: blunt falsehoods are the easiest to catch, and strategic deception the hardest. The second is a validity threat: models that recognise evaluation can change their behaviour, which undermines the measurements meant to reveal deception. We close with twelve open problems and argue that the validity of evaluation should come first.
evidence_items.title: Dissecting Deception in Large Language Models: Mechanisms, Behaviours, and Detection

evidence_items.summary: Direct RNA nanopore sequencing offers the capacity to directly profile native RNAs, enabling detection of diverse epitranscriptomic modifications based on current changes as the RNA passes through a pore. Innovations in chemistry, hardware and bioinformatic tools have increased sequencing capacity and accuracy, creating demand for sequencing multiple samples within individual runs. Two recent solutions enable barcoding and demultiplexing of samples, but independent comparisons of their performance is limited. Here we benchmark WarpDemuX and SeqTagger using orthogonal ground truths derived from species identity and matched IVT spike-ins across four RNA004 flow cells. Both achieve high demultiplexing precision but differ in their trade-offs in precision and retention. SeqTagger provided strong performance at its recommended settings, whilst WarpDemuX performance varied by model, barcode and read quality. IVT-derived score cutoffs allowed dataset-specific calibration and increased WarpDeMux assignment yield, although precision achieved on IVTs was not consistently reproduced in species reads. These results support matched IVTs as internal controls for guiding choice of demultiplexing settings, while demonstrating the need to validate demultiplexing precision in biological RNA populations.
evidence_items.title: Systematic benchmark of demultiplexing workflows for direct RNA sequencing

evidence_items.summary: AI is changing accounting by increasing the speed, accuracy, and analytical capacity of financial operations. This study examines how machine learning, data analytics, robotic process automation, auditing, reporting, forecasting, and professional decision making are used in financial analysis. The study assesses the institutional notification of AI use in accounting as well as its operational advantages. According to the study, artificial intelligence can enhance audit processes, uncover anomalous financial patterns, expedite repetitive activities, assist real-time reporting, and increase the accuracy of financial projections. However, its application also raises issues with algorithmic bias, data quality, information security and accountability for automated decisions. The paper evaluates that while AI can help with accounting procedures, it should not replace the professional skepticism and critical thinking of accounting practitioners. Effective implementation requires strong data governance, explainable algorithms, ongoing human monitoring, ethical standards, and clarity regarding roles. The study also explains the increasing demand for accounting people to acquire knowledge of data analytics, artificial intelligence and ethical technology management. The paper proposes an integrated approach which connects artificial intelligence with accounting applications and governance mechanism. The study concludes that responsible use of AI can improve financial authenticity and accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Ethical Concerns and Operational Implications of Artificial Intelligence in the Accounting Profession

evidence_items.summary: The autonomous navigation of Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) with omnidirectional traction demands precise dynamic models capable of capturing complex phenomena involving friction and lateral slip. This article presents a methodological benchmark evaluating four data-driven system identification strategies: a nonlinear parametric model (Hammerstein), Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV-ARX) systems, the Koopman Operator via Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (EDMD), and Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy). Experimentation was conducted on the Hiwonder ROSOrin hardware, equipped with Mecanum wheels and an onboard Jetson Orin NX edge computing module. To rigorously assess generalization capabilities and penalize parametric overfitting, the primary evaluation was structured under a bidirectional physical domain shift, alternating training and open-loop validation between a high-friction surface (grass) and a low-friction surface (smooth floor). The results demonstrated that EDMD and LPV-ARX achieved comparable global predictive precision across scenarios (RMSE ≈ 0.016–0.018) with inference latencies of ≈0.001ms per step, maintaining consistent cross-domain predictive performance without retraining on the validation surface. In contrast, sparse regression techniques (SINDy) showed weaker cross-domain generalization. The EDMD-Koopman formulation provided comparable predictive performance to LPV-ARX while using a more parsimonious representation (54 active parameters compared to 84 for the LPV). To assess independent-run consistency, an extended validation using 18 independently acquired runs under mixed surface conditions was conducted, providing additional evidence of consistent predictive performance for the dimensional expansion approaches relative to sparse regression. The study concludes by discussing the suitability of EDMD and LPV formulations for future embedded predictive control architectures.
evidence_items.title: Data-Driven Dynamic Identification for Omnidirectional UGVs: A Comparative Benchmark on Generalization and Computational Cost

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Motivation Systems biology strives to unravel the complex dynamics of cellular processes using ordinary differential equations. However, the sparsity of measured data and the strong non-linearity of common ordinary differential equations introduce severe numerical problems in modeling tasks. This motivated the development of computational algorithms that must be systematically evaluated to ensure optimal method choices. The amount of well-curated models for such benchmarking efforts is insufficient, as building and calibrating biologically reasonable models from experiments requires years of work. Results We present a large-scale collection of 1100 synthetic modeling problems, generated based on the systems of ordinary differential equations and experimental designs of 22 published modeling problems. This is achieved by extending a recent method for simulation of time-course data for randomly generated observation functions to also include realistic measurement patterns across multiple experimental conditions. By analyzing data and model characteristics, optimization performance and parameter identifiability, we show that the synthetic problems provide both a realistic and diverse extension of the existing problem space. Hence, the synthetic collection provides a valuable resource for benchmarking in dynamic modeling. Availability and Implementation Benchmark problems and algorithm are publicly available at https://github.com/niklasneubrand/1100SyntheticBenchmarksODE and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23211070.
evidence_items.title: 1100 Synthetic Benchmark Problems for Dynamic Modeling of Cellular Processes

evidence_items.summary: Photovoltaic (PV) plants on legacy monitoring often expose only a cumulative energy counter and partial weather channels, without geolocation or forecasts. We quantify what such data alone can forecast. On two plants (711 and 998 kWp, 18 months), the 15 min target was reconstructed from the counter, and six tree-ensemble families benchmarked as direct forecasters at nine lead times from 15 min to 24 h against four training-free references, under thirty day-stratified Monte Carlo splits, a chronological hold-out and a rolling origin, at task-selected hyperparameters. Skill against seasonal persistence fell from 0.72 at 15 min to 0.49 at 1 h and 0.13–0.17 at 12–24 h; from 30 min to 2 h, diurnal-scaled persistence came within 14% of the best model. No family dominated: the runner-up margin exceeded 1% in only seven of eighteen settings, and task-specific tuning changed the best family in a third of them. Irradiance channels helped only at 15 min. An untransformed target gained up to 14% under random day splits but lost up to 82% on the hold-out, and the earliest rolling origins gave negative skill. The evaluation protocol affects the reported result at least as strongly as the algorithm.
evidence_items.title: Intraday Photovoltaic Energy Forecasting from Legacy Monitoring Data: A Leakage-Free Benchmark of Tree Ensembles Against Persistence References Under Monte Carlo and Chronological Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents two related benchmark studies of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled wake scheduling for ultra-low-power devices in Frequency Range 3 (FR3, 7–24 GHz) ultra-massive multiple-input multiple-output (UM-MIMO) Internet of Things (IoT) networks, evaluated as Pareto-frontier trade-offs between energy and access performance. Study 1 benchmarks wake scheduling for narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) devices under simulated bursty traffic, comparing a classical fixed-interval policy, a genie-aided policy with perfect intensity knowledge, and a learned traffic-intensity estimator, and characterizes the energy–latency frontier together with tail (95th-percentile) latency. Study 2 addresses beam-sweep-aware wake scheduling, in which an idle-mode UM-MIMO IoT device must also account for directional beam-sweep paging overhead, and evaluates listen-window policies against a learned arrival-time predictor on an energy–reliability frontier. In both studies, learned, time-varying state estimates did not uniformly improve on well-designed fixed-policy baselines. They helped in specific regimes, substantially reducing tail latency relative to the genie-aided reference in Study 1 and uniquely reaching near-perfect paging reliability in Study 2, whereas simple classical policies remained preferable elsewhere. The mechanism behind each gain differed between the two problems, indicating that gains from learned prediction are regime- and context-dependent rather than universal.
evidence_items.title: AI-Enabled Wake Scheduling for FR3 Ultra-Massive MIMO IoT Devices: A Simulated Traffic and Beam-Sweep-Aware Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Smartphone-based human activity recognition (HAR) uses features collected from smartphone sensors to distinguish between different human activities. The large number of correlated features generated by smartphone sensors can make feature selection and model interpretation challenging. This study evaluates a two-stage feature selection and classification framework for HAR, in which sparse partial least squares discriminant analysis (sPLS-DA) is used primarily as a supervised feature-selection method, while multinomial logistic regression is employed as the subsequent classifier. The approach is compared with LASSO and Elastic Net regularization under consistent training, testing, and cross-validation procedures. The experiment used 30 repetitions. In each repetition, 21 subjects were used for training and nine subjects were used for testing, with five-fold subject-level cross-validation inside the training set. The original variables selected by each method were evaluated using both unpenalized and Ridge-regularized multinomial logistic regression (MLR) classifiers. Native LASSO and Elastic Net showed similar predictive performance, with mean accuracies of approximately 95%. After expanding the tuning grid, sPLS-DA selected almost all available features, indicating limited sparsity under the investigated tuning range. Using unpenalized MLR on the selected features reduced predictive performance, while Ridge-regularized MLR improved the results for all three feature-selection methods. Overall, the results show that predictive performance, feature-set size, tuning behavior, and the choice of downstream classifier should be considered together when evaluating feature-selection methods for smartphone-based HAR.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable Feature Selection for Smartphone-Based Human Activity Recognition Using Sparse PLS-DA and Multinomial Logistic Regression: A UCI-HAR Benchmark Study

evidence_items.summary: Urban drainage systems rely on fixed surveillance cameras that operate continuously under daytime, nighttime-infrared, rainy, and non-rainy conditions, yet most vision-based water-monitoring methods are validated only on daytime imagery and require costly pixel-level annotation. This paper investigates whether a promptable segmentation foundation model can monitor water surfaces and waterlogging zero-shot—without any task-specific training or labeling—across the full illumination–weather spectrum of real surveillance operations. We construct a benchmark of 3651 frames from 25 fixed cameras of an urban drainage monitoring network in Zhenjiang, China, spanning four scene categories (river/canal, road ponding, underpass, pump-station apron), seven days in July–September 2026, and all four illumination–weather quadrants, explicitly including non-rainy negative days. Using SAM 3 with the text prompt “water”, we extract per-frame water-area ratio and normalized waterline level, and evaluate (i) quadrant-wise segmentation stability, (ii) rain-event detection, (iii) false-alarm behavior on negative days, and (iv) pixel-level agreement with expert reference masks. Zero-shot segmentation met the scene-specific validity criterion on 96.9% of the 162 diurnal-cycle frames at the canal reference site (100% in both no-rain quadrants, 88.9% in the night-rain quadrant); failures concentrate in heavy-rain-obscured and sediment-turbid dusk frames. On 10 August 2026—a day with two visually verified heavy-rain events—the waterline indicator detected both events (peaks 72.9% and 71.4% vs. a 43–62% control-day band), and the same afternoon event was independently corroborated by severe ponding at road and underpass sites city-wide.
evidence_items.title: Zero-Shot Water Monitoring from Fixed Drainage Surveillance Imagery Across Day/Night and Rain/No-Rain Conditions: A SAM 3 Benchmark at 25 Urban Sites

evidence_items.summary: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) provides a versatile promptable segmentation interface, but adverse weather and image degradation can obscure visual cues and substantially reduce its accuracy. Existing approaches mainly follow two directions to mitigate this issue. The first adapts SAM through fine-tuning or additional trainable modules, which requires model-side optimization. The second preprocesses degraded images before SAM inference, but such methods are generally optimized for perceptual restoration rather than downstream segmentation. We introduce WeatherAgent-SAM, an agentic framework that improves degraded-image segmentation through response-conditioned preprocessing selection while keeping SAM frozen. WeatherAgent-SAM takes SAM’s initial response and a spatial prompt as inputs and uses response-conditioned knowledge to determine which preprocessing method should be applied next. To realize this process, the framework comprises two key modules. First, Fine-Grained Response-Conditioned Knowledge Construction adopts a progressive coarse-to-fine strategy: it first categorizes SAM responses into recurring states and then explores how individual preprocessing methods affect segmentation within each state. This design enables the agent to distinguish methods that pursue similar enhancement objectives but produce different segmentation outcomes. Second, a learnable Mask Verifier estimates the quality of each resulting SAM mask without ground truth and provides feedback to the agent, allowing tool selection to proceed iteratively and stop when a satisfactory prediction is identified. Experiments demonstrate that WeatherAgent-SAM achieves results comparable to those of the evaluated baselines on the Robust-Seg dataset and outperforms SAM, RobustSAM, and GaRA-SAM-Syn on the ACDC dataset.
evidence_items.title: WeatherAgent-SAM: Text-Grounded Agentic Tool Selection for Robust SAM Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Paired benchmark of local language model generation speed on one HP Notebook (Intel Core i3-5005U, 2 cores / 4 threads, 6 GB RAM, Intel HD Graphics 5500). The laptop was tested under Windows 10 Home 22H2 (build 19045) on 2026-09-29, then under Linux Mint 22.3 "Zena" (Cinnamon 6.6.4, kernel 6.14.0-37-generic) on 2026-10-10. Both runs used Ollama 0.11.4 and the same tinyllama Q4 0 model (digest 2644915ede352ea7bdfaff0bfac0be74c719d5d5202acb63a6fb095b52f394a4), CPU-only (num gpu: 0), temperature 0, seed 42 and num predict 200: one cold request after unloading the model, then three warm requests. Results: median warm generation throughput was 12.9 tokens/s on Linux Mint and 9.4 tokens/s on Windows 10 (+37.2%, ratio 1.37). Cold full-answer completion took 19.8 s on Mint and 229.8 s on Windows; the Windows figure includes about 167 s of Ollama runner startup. Ollama reported 0.7 GB of loaded model memory on both systems. Limitations: this is a paired whole-system comparison and does not isolate the operating system as the cause. Windows had desktop applications and the Ollama tray app running; background activity and the power profile on Mint during inference were not recorded. Each system has three warm runs from a single session, and individual run rates were not retained, so variability cannot be estimated. Files: linux-mint-report-20261010.md (method, results, calculations and limitations); windows.csv and linux-mint-cinnamon-20261010-144025.csv (aggregate results per operating system); bench.py (the benchmark script, unmodified, from repository commit 491c71a).

evidence_items.summary: This repository benchmarks 11 AI models on a task customs brokers do every day: assigning the tariff code (HTS) to a product from its description alone. The ground truth is 1,098 binding rulings issued by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP CROSS, New York) between January and August 2026, with duty rates taken from the USITC tariff schedule. Models range from small free ones to Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol. Every model is graded on the same 228 rulings dated after the latest training cutoff among them (July to mid-August 2026), so no model is compared on easier or possibly memorised material. A second table uses all 1,098 rulings as an upper bound. Main findings: (1) Even the best models get the 8-digit code that sets the duty right only about half the time (Claude Opus 5.5 53.5%, GPT-6 Sol 49.1% on the same 228; the two are statistically tied). (2) The small free models score under 6%. (3) The best models’ errors are mostly real codes for the wrong product, so a “does this code exist?” check catches only about a third of them. (4) When a wrong code changes the duty, most models lean toward underpaying (7 of 11 beat a chance baseline); Claude Opus 5.5 does not show it. Dollar figures use base (MFN) duty only, so they are a minimum. Limits: base duty only (no Section 301 or 232), New York rulings only, models answer from the description with no tariff lookup, four models have no stated training cutoff, and reasoning could not be switched off for some. Analysis plans were pre-registered and every deviation is logged. Includes the data, code, prompts, per-ruling model outputs and a script that verifies every number in the README.
evidence_items.title: Tariff Cost Benchmark: Duty-at-Stake and Direction Bias in LLM Customs Classification

organizations: Department of Neurosurgery and Neurotechnology, Eberhard Karls University, 72076 Tuebingen, Germany
evidence_items.summary: Retrospective clinical research depends on reliable extraction of structured variables from unstructured medical documentation, but manual chart abstraction is slow and vulnerable to inter-rater variability. We compared zero-shot extraction of clinically relevant variables from German neurosurgical records by large language models (LLMs) with extraction by two human auditors. We analyzed 881 de-identified clinical notes from 211 patients undergoing microvascular decompression and extracted 15 predefined binary variables across three domains: preoperative symptoms, postoperative complications, and disease course. Six LLMs were assessed, including cloud-based models (GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude Sonnet 3.5, and Gemini 2.0 Flash) and locally hosted models (llama 3.3 and deepseek-r1), with three runs per patient record. Outputs were compared with two independent human auditors against a clinician-adjudicated reference standard. Cloud-based models had higher observed F1 scores than the local models across all three domains. GPT-4o achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for preoperative symptoms; GPT-4o, o3-mini, and Gemini 2.0 Flash reached F1 scores of 0.65–0.68 for postoperative complications; and Sonnet 3.5 achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for disease course. These findings suggest that zero-shot LLM prompting could be a scalable approach for clinical information extraction while emphasizing persistent limitations in rare-event detection and privacy-sensitive deployment.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Information Extraction from Neurosurgical Clinical Notes: A Benchmark Against Human Auditors

evidence_items.summary: Leveraging auxiliary textual data can help with user profiling and item characterization in recommender systems (RSs). However, incomplete user and item descriptions limit the potential of textual information. To this end, we propose a graph-aware convolutional large language model (LLM) method, eliciting LLMs to summarize from a high-order interaction graph to generate fine-grained descriptions for users and items. We focus on two challenges in this paper: 1) the incompatibility between structural graph and text-aware LLMs . Although some work converts graph data into textual form using templates and sampling strategies, they limit the LLMs’ ability to maintain a global perspective on graphs for LLM reasoning. 2) the limitation of LLMs’ capability for long context. Simply describing a large-scale graph in a textual format makes LLM struggle to robustly comprehend information from lengthy contextual inputs. To bridge the gap between graph structures and LLMs, we employ the LLM as an aggregator for the graph convolution process, eliciting it to aggregate and refine the graph-based information iteratively. To mitigate the information overload associated with large-scale graphs, we segment the graph processing into manageable steps, progressively incorporating multi-hop information in a least-to-most manner. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.
evidence_items.title: GaCLLM: Large Language Model with Graph Convolution for Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models require reproducible outputs for systematic evaluation in tumor boards. We developed a sarcoma tumor-board simulator using Claude Opus 4.5 at temperature 0.0, schema-enforced JSON output, and prompt-specified semantic and conditional-logic rules. The framework was evaluated on 51 de-identified cases across 154 runs. Reproducibility was defined as agreement across all runs of a case per decision code. In the 41 cases not used during development, reproducibility was 94.2% (cluster-bootstrap 95% CI 91.9–96.1); in the 10 development cases, 93.3% (95% CI 88.6–97.6). Pooled, it was 94.0% (95% CI 92.0–95.8); 17 cases agreed on all 21 codes. Estimates are model-specific. A post hoc ablation on 15 cases compared the framework with and without these rules: 94.6% versus 82.5% (difference 12.1 points; 95% CI 7.6–17.1). The improvement was driven mainly by exact wording agreement in three free-text fields (+ 60.0 points), whereas the 18 categorical and numeric codes differed by 4.1 points (95% CI − 0.7 to 9.3). Without any schema, a decision was stated for only 37.6% of instances versus 100% under schema enforcement; seven codes were never addressed. Single-reviewer screening detected no fabricated numbers, references, or measurements. Clinical correctness was not assessed. Consistent recommendations may still be incorrect.
evidence_items.title: A schema-enforced large language model framework produces largely reproducible decision codes in simulated sarcoma tumor boards

evidence_items.summary: Session-based recommendation (SBR) predicts the next item based on anonymous sessions. Traditional SBR explores user intents based on ID collaborations or auxiliary content. To further alleviate data sparsity and cold-start issues, recent Multimodal SBR (MSBR) methods utilize simplistic pre-trained models for modality learning but have limitations in semantic richness. Considering the semantic reasoning abilities of multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) and the practical request for high inference efficiency, we focus on the LLM-enhanced MSBR scenario in this paper, which leverages LLM cognition for comprehensive multimodal representation generation, to enhance downstream MSBR. Tackling this problem faces two challenges: i) how to obtain LLM cognition on both inherent multimodal knowledge and transitional patterns, ii) how to align transitional patterns and inherent knowledge into one unified LLM without increasing inference complexity. To this end, we propose a multimodal LLM-enhanced framework TPAD, which extends a teacher-student distillation paradigm to decouple and align transitional patterns for promoting MSBR. TPAD establishes parallel Knowledge-MLLM and Transfer-MLLM, where the former as student model interprets item knowledge-reflected features and the latter as teacher model extracts transition-aware features. Transitional pattern alignment harnessing mutual information estimation unites two MLLMs, distilling transitional patterns into representations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TPAD. Implementation codes are available at https://github.com/TiliaceaeSU/TPAD .
evidence_items.title: Distilling Transitional Patterns to Multimodal Large Language Models for Session-based Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in legal information systems, yet their knowledge is not uniformly distributed across legal domains. We introduce a knowledge-probe pipeline that measures whether an LLM exhibits differential confidence across areas of law. Applying the pipeline to 1,200 court decisions across three jurisdictions (Germany, France, Canada), we find that Llama 3.3 70B systematically under-hedges on social welfare law relative to tax law in non-English jurisdictions: 49.8% of tax probes elicit admitted uncertainty vs. only 6.8% for social welfare in Germany (p < 0.0001), with a smaller but significant gap in France (p = 0.003) and no gap in Canada (English). The pattern is consistent with the representation of each language in training corpora and replicates on Qwen3 32B. The model achieves comparable accuracy in both domains, yet signals false confidence precisely in the legal areas that serve socioeconomically vulnerable populations. A retrieval-augmented intervention, providing related legal text at query time, closes 87% of the gap, suggesting the overconfidence stems from a knowledge deficit. We frame this as a form of compounding injustice: already marginalized users receive confidently stated but unreliable information in legal areas that are historically underserved and underrepresented in NLP, with no signal that the system's knowledge is thinner in their area of need than in other areas of law, which are much better hedged.
evidence_items.title: Selective Overconfidence: How Large Language Models Underserve Social Welfare Law Across Jurisdictions

organizations: DOE Joint Genome Institute, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
evidence_items.summary: Reliable classification of transposable elements (TEs) is important for genome annotation and evolutionary analysis, yet remains challenging: TE families differ widely across taxa, reference databases label them inconsistently, and many TEs are represented only by degraded copies. We introduce GLARE (Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification), a TE classifier built by fine-tuning a genomic language model on harmonized PanTEon and Repbase reference data to predict TE superfamily across 32 superfamilies in 11 orders. Among the genomic language models compared, Nucleotide Transformer v3 provided the strongest representation. Built on this backbone, GLARE exceeded all nine classifiers in the PanTEon benchmark, reaching 0.966 weighted superfamily F1 on its 30-superfamily task. GLARE also showed stronger generalization to clades absent from training, consistently exceeding state-of-the-art classifiers on holdouts spanning three taxonomic ranks: the order Poales, the phylum Arthropoda, and the kingdom Fungi. Training on both PanTEon and Repbase reduced the performance drop seen when a single-source model was applied to the other database. Under simulated sequence decay, GLARE was the most robust classifier tested, and it performed best on independently curated degraded libraries. These findings show that genomic language models fine-tuned on harmonized multi-source references can classify TEs robustly under the taxonomic, database, and sequence-quality shifts that matter in practice. GLARE is available at https://code.jgi.doe.gov/NHaas/glare.
evidence_items.title: GLARE: Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification

evidence_items.summary: Explaining anomalies in spatiotemporal data requires more than identifying statistical deviations; it often demands coherent narratives that relate events to their spatial, temporal, and social context. In urban settings, where anomalies may reflect public events, behavioral shifts, or environmental factors, the lack of interpretable, contextual explanations limits the effectiveness of automated analysis. We present GroundSTory , an interactive framework that reframes spatiotemporal anomaly explanation as computational storytelling, integrating graph-based representations of urban space, coordinated visual analytics, and large language models (LLMs) to support the construction of grounded, human-readable narrative explanations. Anomalies act as narrative anchors, while localized spatial and temporal relations and contextual signals derived from the graph guide and constrain narrative generation. The LLM functions as a narrative assistant, proposing plausible, evidence-backed hypotheses that analysts can inspect, compare, and validate through visual interaction. We illustrate the approach through qualitative usage scenarios on real-world urban datasets from São Paulo and New York City, showing how interactive narratives surface meaningful links between detected anomalies and contextual factors such as holidays, mass events, and routine activity patterns. A prompt analysis further suggests that structured, graph-derived context tends to affect the stability and perceived quality of generated hypotheses. Overall, our results indicate that combining knowledge-driven representations, interactive visualization, and constrained prompting can support more coherent, plausible, and interpretable narratives for spatiotemporal anomaly analysis, contributing to ongoing research in interactive storytelling and narrative-centered AI systems.
evidence_items.title: GroundSTory: Interactive Storytelling for Grounded Spatiotemporal Anomaly Explanations with Graphs and Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Patients considering robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) require information that spans diagnosis, treatment selection, functional recovery, and recurrence surveillance. We compared the quality of English-language RARP patient education generated by ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao. Twenty-five questions covering screening, diagnosis, treatment decision-making, perioperative care, rehabilitation, and follow-up were submitted individually to each model, yielding 75 responses. Three blinded clinicians evaluated the responses using the Global Quality Score, modified DISCERN, Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence, Ensuring Quality Information for Patients, and the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool; six readability indices were also calculated. Overall Global Quality Scores did not differ significantly across models. ChatGPT achieved a higher EQIP score (median, 75.00%) than DeepSeek and Doubao (65.83% each) and greater PEMAT actionability (59.00% vs. 54.33% and 47.67%, respectively). DeepSeek generated comparatively easier-to-read text, although all three models exceeded commonly recommended sixth- to eighth-grade reading levels for public-facing health materials. Under the majority-rater criterion, no factual errors or outdated recommendations were identified, whereas key omissions occurred mainly in DeepSeek and Doubao responses. Inter-rater agreement was low, indicating substantial uncertainty in multidimensional human assessment. LLMs may support the preparation of clinician-reviewed RARP educational materials but should not replace individualized counseling by urologists.
evidence_items.title: Large language models differ in patient education quality across the robot-assisted radical prostatectomy care pathway

organizations: University of Kansas

evidence_items.summary: This special issue brings together 11 manuscripts that examine the evolving role of artificial intelligence (AI) in research-based educational products and practices, with particular attention to students with disabilities and the educators who support them. Across empirical studies, systematic and theoretical reviews, and technology-in-action pieces, contributing authors explore how AI can support implementation fidelity, professional development, writing instruction, mathematics, personalized learning, coaching, feedback, accessibility, and educational technology development. Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for educators, researchers, or human judgment, this issue emphasizes human-centered design, evidence-based implementation, transparency, accessibility, and ongoing evaluation. Collectively, the articles highlight both the opportunities and limitations of AI, underscoring the need for responsible innovation that improves usability, feasibility, effectiveness, and equity while carefully addressing concerns about privacy, bias, reliability, and academic integrity.
evidence_items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Research-Based Educational Products

evidence_items.summary: Significance: There is potential for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to perform "full stack" academic publishing, including comprehensive manuscript fabrication, "peer"-review, and editorial decision making. This study evaluated the benefits and cautions in using AI for full stack academic publishing in clinical research about seizures. Methods: Three epileptologists each selected 1 published manuscript in Epilepsia and produced an AI-fabricated manuscript about seizures. AI tools were then used to perform "peer"-review and make editorial decisions with minimal human supervision. The rates of identifying AI-fabricated manuscripts and editorial decisions among the epileptologists was analyzed, and epileptologists' observations on how AI differed from typical human "peer"-review and editorial decisions was collected. Results: Four of 6 (67%) pairs of AI-fabricated and human-generated manuscripts were correctly identified. Only 1 AI-fabricated manuscript was editorially rejected, whereas another had a subtle indicator of fabrication. When compared to human content, AI generated content was comprehensive, detailed, and based on the highest standard of academic publication. However, generated content was more verbose, used more structured responses, and more critical feedback. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that the quality of AI-fabricated manuscripts about clinical research in seizures was sufficiently high that the current methods of peer and editorial review could not easily distinguish fabricated content compared to human-written content. Moreover, AI review and editorial decisions were high quality and appeared reasonable in many cases. AI tools have matured to the point that there should be thoughtful policies that permit AI assistance but prohibit insufficiently supervised autonomous scientific submissions, reviews, and editorial decisions.
evidence_items.title: Full stack academic publishing in seizures with artificial intelligence: a cautionary tale

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is of great importance for the renewable energy conversion to hydrogen fuel via water electrolysis. However, the current benchmark Pt/C catalyst suffers from high cost, pH sensitivity, and deficient durability, severely restricting the large‐scale development of membrane water electrolysis. Herein, we develop a cost‐effective Pt‐free catalyst featuring high‐density, ultrafine Ru nanoclusters modified with CoP and uniformly dispersed on nitrogen‐doped carbon films (NCF). This catalyst achieves not only superior HER activity across a wide pH range but also robust stability at ampere‐level large current densities, manifesting as a competitive alternative to commercial Pt/C. Typically, Ru‐CoP/NCF exhibits an overpotential of only 22 mV at 10 mA cm −2 in acidic media, with the mass activity and price activity 1.21 and 2.18 times higher than Pt/C, respectively. A proton exchange membrane water electrolyzer using Ru‐CoP/NCF catalyst delivers a high current density of 1.0 A cm −2 at a voltage of merely 1.67 V and sustains long‐term operation for 780 h with a minimal decay rate of 84 µV h −1 . This Ru‐CoP/NCF catalyst thus demonstrates practical potential for the development of non‐Pt membrane electrodes.
evidence_items.title: High‐Density‐Cluster Ru Catalyst Substitute for Pt/C Benchmark Improves Membrane Water Electrolysis

evidence_items.summary: Heavy metal contamination represents a persistent environmental concern because of the long-term stability, mobility, and potential bioavailability of these contaminants in water, soils, and sediments. Anthropogenic activities, including mining, metallurgical and industrial processes, agriculture, energy production, and waste disposal, can substantially increase metal concentrations above natural geochemical background levels, with potential consequences for ecosystem functioning and human health. This critical narrative review examines current remediation strategies, with particular emphasis on biological approaches and microbially induced carbonate precipitation (MICP). The relevant literature was identified through a structured, topic-driven search in Scopus and Google Scholar using the keywords “MICP” and “heavy metals”, individually and in combination, and was selected according to its relevance to remediation mechanisms, process performance, environmental constraints, technological limitations, and field-scale applicability. The review distinguishes the major biological mechanisms involved in metal remediation, including biosorption, bioaccumulation, biotransformation, phytoremediation, and biomineralization, and critically evaluates their advantages and limitations. Attention is given to carbonate-associated metal immobilization by MICP and to its application to cadmium remediation, while comparative evidence for other metals is also considered. Although high removal efficiencies have been reported for MICP under controlled laboratory conditions, their direct extrapolation to complex environmental matrices remains constrained by metal speciation, pH, salinity, microbial activity, reagent requirements, ammonium generation, and long-term mineral stability.
evidence_items.title: Sustainable Microbial Bioremediation of Heavy Metal Contamination: Mechanisms, Microbially Induced Carbonate Precipitation, Limitations, and Future Perspectives

evidence_items.summary: The long-term environmental legacy of historical gold mining continues to pose significant concerns about water quality and human health. This study evaluates and compares the impacts of former gold mines on groundwater (GW) and surface water (SW) quality, and the associated human health risks, at the Crocette/Pestarena mining district (Italy) and the Jales mine (Portugal), characterized by different post-closure conditions. Hydrochemical data from three sampling campaigns in Italy and a single campaign in Portugal were integrated with pollution indices (Heavy Metal Pollution Index, HPI; Heavy Metal Evaluation Index, HEI; and Water Pollution Index, WPI) and a Human Health Risk Assessment (HHRA) under different exposure scenarios. Arsenic was identified as the main contaminant, exceeding drinking water standards in 75% of the Italian and 53% of the Portuguese samples. Exceedances were also recorded for Al, Cd, Fe, Mn, Ni and Pb. The pollution indices identified localized GW pollution downstream of the tailings in Italy, whereas more diffuse pollution, affecting both GW and SW, was observed downstream of the tailings and the passive water treatment system in Portugal. The HHRA revealed unacceptable non-carcinogenic and carcinogenic risks for GW ingestion in both study areas, primarily driven by As. In contrast, risks associated with recreational exposure to SW through ingestion and dermal contact remained within acceptable thresholds. These findings highlight the importance of long-term monitoring and effective intervention strategies to manage water resources in areas persistently impacted by former mining activities.
evidence_items.title: Tracing the Legacy of Gold Mining: Comparative Insights into Water Contamination and Human Health Risks in Italy and Portugal

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Clinical communication is central to patient outcomes, yet large-scale annotation of patient–provider conversations remains labor-intensive, inconsistent, and difficult to scale. Existing large language model (LLM)–based approaches typically rely on single-task systems with limited robustness across communication frameworks and clinical domains. In this study, we developed MOSAIC, a M ulti-framew O rk S tructured Agentic AI system for scalable Clinical C ommunication coding. MOSAIC combines dynamically few-shot prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow for planning, annotation, and verification. Performance was evaluated against gold-standard annotations produced by trained human coders. MOSAIC was developed on 54 annotated transcripts and evaluated on 120 transcripts spanning rheumatology and obstetrics/gynecology (OB/GYN). On the evaluation set, MOSAIC achieved an overall weighted F1 score of 95.6%. Performance was highest in rheumatology (F1 = 95.9%) and strongest for bias and patient behaviors categories (F1 = 96.4% and 96.1%, respectively). These results demonstrate the potential of multi-framework AI systems for reliable clinical communication analysis.
evidence_items.title: An agentic AI system for multi-framework communication coding

evidence_items.summary: Agentic AI is reconfiguring service systems by introducing computational entities that interpret situations, select among alternatives, and shape service trajectories with varying degrees of decision authority. Established service-design representations lack a category for such entities, treating them either as passive artifacts or as human actors. Following design science research, this paper develops a design theory for modeling algorithmic actors in agentic service systems. It comprises a four-level framework—service-system embedding, actor differentiation, decision authority, and responsible AI governance—with operational classification rules, five design principles for materiality, and testable propositions. The theory is instantiated as an extension of service blueprinting and formatively evaluated in three real-world configurations whose primary algorithmic actors hold assistive, delegated, and autonomous authority with different forms of embodiment. Interviews with six informants, documents, and observations provide preliminary evidence that the extended blueprint can represent algorithmic actors, authority allocations, authority transitions, and governance mechanisms at the process-step level. The cases illustrate that the same algorithmic actor can hold different authority levels across process steps and suggest two propositions for future testing: that risk types vary with embodiment and that escalation architectures become more elaborate as authority increases.
evidence_items.title: From Artifacts to Actors: A Design Theory for Modeling Algorithmic Actors in Agentic Service Systems

evidence_items.summary: Many industrial vision questions are binary ("is this suitcase damaged?") and must be answered on premises, with a confidence that can be trusted and an option to defer to a human. We study how far small open vision-language models (VLMs) get on such questions and what it takes to make them reliable. First, a pre-registered benchmark of 12 open VLMs (0.8B-12B parameters; 1,807 yes/no items in four question families; test split analysed once) on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin finds flat discrimination among the Qwen-based models of 2B parameters and above (pooled test AUROC 0.930-0.940), no gain from models post-trained for decisions over their own base models, and calibration that varies far more across models than ranking does: raw expected calibration error ranges from 0.014 to 0.122, and one shared Platt step brings every model to 0.013-0.037. Qwen3-VL-2B is the fastest model (0.45 s per image, 4.4 GB), and no model was significantly better than it in any tested comparison. Second, we attach per-task heads, L2-regularised logistic regressions on the frozen model's last-layer hidden state, and abstain below a confidence threshold set by the application. On test photos from sources unseen in training, a suitcase-damage head raises AUROC from 0.925 (calibrated model answer) to 0.962, paired 95% CI of the gain [+0.018, +0.058]; at a 0.90 threshold it answers 71.7% of the photos with 96.6% accuracy, against 61.1% for the calibrated answer. A baggage-presence head does not improve AUROC. Third, a case study runs the calibrated model on an 8 GB laptop: on 148 test photos it decides 49% automatically at 97.3% accuracy and leaves the rest to staff, at no API cost. Limitations: internet photos only, four question families, and a source confound in one damage test set.
evidence_items.title: Calibrated Yes/No Visual Decisions with Small Open Vision-Language Models: A Pre-Registered Benchmark of 12 Models, Plug-In Heads, and an Airline Baggage Case Study
